annotation.targetText: In brief, dialectics can be defined as the doctrine of the unity of opposites. This embodies the essence of dialectics, but it requires explanations and development.
annotation.summary: Lenin's famous core definition of dialectics: reality develops not through external mechanistic pushes, but through the internal contradictory forces inherent in every phenomenon.
annotation.explanation: Lenin's famous core definition of dialectics: reality develops not through external mechanistic pushes, but through the internal contradictory forces inherent in every phenomenon.

annotation.targetText: 1) The objectivity of consideration (not examples, not divergencies, but the Thing-in-itself).
annotation.summary: Dialectics begins with objective materialist rigor: analyzing the object in its own internal properties and lawful motion, rather than selecting subjective or superficial illustrations.
annotation.explanation: Dialectics begins with objective materialist rigor: analyzing the object in its own internal properties and lawful motion, rather than selecting subjective or superficial illustrations.

annotation.targetText: 5) The thing (phenomenon, etc.) as the sum and unity of opposites.
annotation.summary: Every material process is an internal unity of mutually conditioning and mutually exclusive tendencies that constitute its identity and drive its change.
annotation.explanation: Every material process is an internal unity of mutually conditioning and mutually exclusive tendencies that constitute its identity and drive its change.

annotation.targetText: 11) The endless process of the deepening of man's knowledge of the thing, of phenomena, processes, etc., from appearance to essence and from less profound to more profound essence.
annotation.summary: Lenin outlines the dialectical materialist theory of reflection: human cognition is an infinite historical process penetrating deeper beyond superficial appearances into the essential lawful contradictions of nature and society.
annotation.explanation: Lenin outlines the dialectical materialist theory of reflection: human cognition is an infinite historical process penetrating deeper beyond superficial appearances into the essential lawful contradictions of nature and society.

annotation.targetText: The splitting of a single whole and the cognition of its contradictory parts (see the quotation from Philo on Heraclitus at the beginning of Section III, “On Cognition,” in Lasalle’s book on Heraclitus[1]) is the essence (one of the “essentials,” one of the principal, if not the principal, characteristics or features) of dialectics.
annotation.summary: Lenin traces dialectics from ancient Greek philosophy (Heraclitus) through Hegel to Marx, identifying its primary principle: analyzing any phenomenon requires discovering its internally divided, contradictory aspects.
annotation.explanation: Lenin traces dialectics from ancient Greek philosophy (Heraclitus) through Hegel to Marx, identifying its primary principle: analyzing any phenomenon requires discovering its internally divided, contradictory aspects.

annotation.targetText: The two basic (or two possible? Or two historically observable?) conceptions of development (evolution) are: development as decrease and increase, as repetition, and development as a unity of opposites (the division of a unity into mutually exclusive opposites and their reciprocal relation).
annotation.summary: Lenin contrasts vulgar evolutionism with revolutionary dialectics. The former views change merely as gradual quantitative growth without breaks or leaps; the latter identifies the source of motion within the internal struggle of opposites.
annotation.explanation: Lenin contrasts vulgar evolutionism with revolutionary dialectics. The former views change merely as gradual quantitative growth without breaks or leaps; the latter identifies the source of motion within the internal struggle of opposites.
annotation.context: Following the collapse of the Second International in 1914, Lenin retreated to the Bern library to study Hegel. He realized that reformists like Plekhanov and Kautsky had abandoned dialectics for vulgar, mechanical evolutionism, which led them to preach class collaboration and support the imperialist war.

annotation.targetText: The first conception is lifeless, pale and dry. The second is living. The second alone furnishes the key to the “self-movement” of everything existing; it alone furnishes the key to “leaps,” to the “break in continuity,” to the “transformation into the opposite,” to the destruction of the old and the emergence of the new.
annotation.summary: Dialectics alone explains qualitative transformations and revolutionary ruptures in history. Without the unity of opposites, motion must be attributed to an external cause or metaphysical prime mover.
annotation.explanation: Dialectics alone explains qualitative transformations and revolutionary ruptures in history. Without the unity of opposites, motion must be attributed to an external cause or metaphysical prime mover.

annotation.targetText: The unity (coincidence, identity, equal action) of opposites is conditional, temporary, transitory, relative. The struggle of mutually exclusive opposites is absolute, just as development and motion are absolute.
annotation.summary: A fundamental law of dialectical materialism: equilibrium and stability are always temporary and relative, while contradiction, struggle, and historical transformation are eternal and absolute.
annotation.explanation: A fundamental law of dialectical materialism: equilibrium and stability are always temporary and relative, while contradiction, struggle, and historical transformation are eternal and absolute.

annotation.targetText: Human knowledge is not (or does not follow) a straight line, but a curve, which endlessly approximates a series of circles, a spiral.

annotation.targetText: Who are our enemies? Who are our friends? This is a question of the first importance for the revolution.
annotation.summary: Revolutionary strategy begins with concrete class analysis to distinguish true allies from class enemies.
annotation.explanation: Mao opens Volume I of his Selected Works by establishing that revolutionary strategy begins with concrete class analysis. Without accurately identifying which social classes have a material interest in overthrowing imperialism and feudalism and which classes benefit from maintaining exploitation, a revolutionary party inevitably isolates itself or surrenders leadership to vacillating bourgeois allies.
annotation.context: In anti-colonial struggles across the Global South, movements that failed to distinguish between national-popular allies and foreign-backed comprador elites were repeatedly betrayed from within once formal independence was achieved.

annotation.targetText: In economically backward and semi-colonial China the landlord class and the comprador class are wholly appendages of the international bourgeoisie, depending upon imperialism for their survival and growth.
annotation.summary: In semi-colonial countries, domestic landlords and comprador capitalists are direct appendages of foreign imperialism.
annotation.explanation: Mao defines the comprador bourgeoisie and feudal landlord class as structural extensions of foreign monopoly capital inside an oppressed nation. Unlike an independent industrial bourgeoisie, compradors act as commercial and financial middlemen extracting wealth from domestic workers and peasants on behalf of foreign imperialist powers.
annotation.context: Modern comprador elites in Latin America, Africa, and Asia manage local subsidiaries, export enclaves, and privatized utilities for Western multinationals while relying on foreign military aid to suppress domestic labor unions.

annotation.targetText: The middle bourgeoisie, by which is meant chiefly the national bourgeoisie, [3] is inconsistent in its attitude towards the Chinese revolution: they feel the need for revolution and favour the revolutionary movement against imperialism and the warlords when they are smarting under the blows of foreign capital and the oppression of the warlords, but they become suspicious of the revolution when they sense that, with the militant participation of the proletariat at home and the active support of the international proletariat abroad, the revolution is threatening the hope of their class to attain the status of a big bourgeoisie.
annotation.summary: The national bourgeoisie in semi-colonial nations is caught in a contradiction: it resents foreign imperialist domination but fears working-class militancy.
annotation.explanation: Mao formulates the classic Marxist analysis of the dual character of the national bourgeoisie in semi-colonial countries. Because foreign monopolies restrict their domestic market, national capitalists intermittently support anti-imperialist struggles; however, because they themselves exploit wage labor, they panic whenever working-class and peasant organization threatens private property, causing their right wing to defect to imperialism (as Chiang Kai-shek did in the 1927 Shanghai massacre).
annotation.context: Domestic manufacturing owners in developing countries often support state tariffs against foreign imports, yet quickly ally with right-wing coups or IMF austerity programs when domestic workers strike for higher wages.

annotations.bookTitle: Analysis of the Classes in Chinese Society

annotation.targetText: Though not very numerous, the industrial proletariat represents China's new productive forces, is the most progressive class in modern China and has become the leading force in the revolutionary movement.
annotation.summary: Despite its smaller size in an agrarian country, the industrial working class is the vanguard leader of the revolution due to its concentration in modern industry and total lack of private property.
annotation.explanation: Refuting mechanical determinists who argued that China's industrial working class was too small to lead a revolution, Mao explains why the proletariat exercises vanguard leadership: first, its high concentration in large-scale modern enterprises (railways, mines, shipping, and textiles), and second, its complete deprivation of means of production under triple oppression by imperialists, warlords, and capitalists.
annotation.context: During the 1922 to 1926 Hong Kong-Canton, railway, and Shanghai general strikes, China's two million industrial workers paralyzed foreign imperialist commerce and spearheaded the national liberation movement.

annotation.targetText:
The cornerstone of anarchism is the individual, whose emancipation, 
according to its tenets, is the principal condition for the emancipation of the 
masses, the collective body. According to the tenets of anarchism, the emancipation 
of the masses is impossible until the individual is emancipated. Accordingly, its 
slogan is: "Everything for the individual." The cornerstone of Marxism, however, 
is the masses, whose emancipation, according to its tenets, is the principal condition 
for the emancipation of the individual. That is to say, according to the tenets 
of Marxism, the emancipation of the individual is impossible until the masses are 
emancipated. Accordingly, its slogan is: "Everything for the masses."
annotation.summary: Contrasts the individualist premise of anarchism with the collective foundation of scientific socialism.
annotation.explanation: Anarchism places the isolated individual at its center, asserting that social emancipation occurs only after individual liberation. Marxism inverts this premise: individual freedom is materially impossible so long as the mass of humanity remains bound by capitalist exploitation. Genuine individual emancipation requires collective class liberation.
annotation.context: Written in Tiflis between late 1906 and early 1907 during the reactionary aftermath of the 1905 Russian Revolution, when Georgian anarchist groups under V. Cherkezishvili were winning influence among Caucasian workers.

annotation.targetText:
Socialism is divided into three main trends : reformism, anarchism and Marxism.

Reformism (Bernstein and others), which regards socialism as a remote goal and 
nothing more, reformism, which actually repudiates the socialist revolution and 
aims at establishing socialism by peaceful means, reformism, which advocates not 
class struggle but class collaboration : this reformism is decaying day by day, is 
day by day losing all semblance of socialism and, in our opinion, it is totally 
unnecessary to examine it in these articles when defining socialism.

It is altogether different with Marxism and anarchism: both are at the present 
time recognised as socialist trends, they are waging a fierce struggle against each 
other, both are trying to present themselves to the proletariat as genuinely socialist 
doctrines, and, of course, a study and comparison of the two will be far more interesting 
for the reader.

We are not the kind of people who, when the word "anarchism" is mentioned, turn 
away contemptuously and say with a supercilious wave of the hand: "Why waste time 
on that, it's not worth talking about!" We think that such cheap "criticism" is 
undignified and useless.

Nor are we the kind of people who console themselves with the thought that the 
Anarchists "have no masses behind them and, therefore, are not so dangerous." It 
is not who has a larger or smaller "mass" following today, but the essence of the 
doctrine that matters. If the "doctrine" of the Anarchists expresses the truth, 
then it goes without saying that it will certainly hew a path for itself and will 
rally the masses around itself. If, however, it is unsound and built up on a false 
foundation, it will not last long and will remain suspended in mid-air. But the 
unsoundness of anarchism must be proved.

Some people believe that Marxism and anarchism are based on the same principles 
and that the disagreements between them concern only tactics, so that, in the opinion 
of these people, it is quite impossible to draw a contrast between these two trends.

This is a great mistake.

We believe that the Anarchists are real enemies of Marxism. Accordingly, we also 
hold that a real struggle must be waged against real enemies. Therefore, it is necessary 
to examine the "doctrine" of the Anarchists from beginning to end and weigh it up 
thoroughly from all aspects.
annotation.summary: Distinguishes Marxism from both bourgeois reformism and petty-bourgeois anarchism.
annotation.explanation: Categorizes modern socialism into three distinct currents: reformism (class collaboration and denial of revolution), anarchism (individualist repudiation of the state and class discipline), and Marxism (scientific class struggle culminating in the dictatorship of the proletariat).
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotation.targetText:
It is true that the rural and urban petty bourgeoisie 
now constitute the majority and are really poor, but is that the point? The petty 
bourgeoisie has long constituted the majority, but up to now it has displayed no 
initiative in the struggle for "freedom" without the assistance of the proletariat. 
Why? Because the petty bourgeoisie as a class is not growing; on the contrary, it 
is disintegrating day by day and breaking up into bourgeois and proletarians.
annotation.summary: The petty bourgeoisie disintegrates under capitalism while the proletariat steadily expands.
annotation.explanation: Refutes the populist argument that socialists should orient toward the petty bourgeoisie merely because of its numerical size. Small producers and shopkeepers are being steadily ruined and proletarianized by capitalist competition. Dialectics aligns with the proletariat because it represents the ascendant, growing class of the future.

annotation.targetText: Louis Blanc, the French socialist, won unenviable notriety during the revolution of 1848 by changing his stand from that of the class struggle to that of petty-bourgeois illusions, illusions adorned with would-be “socialist” phraseology, but in reality tending to strengthen the influence of the bourgeoisie over the proletariat.
annotation.summary: Lenin defines Blancism: the historical tendency of moderate socialists to abandon independent class struggle, enter capitalist ministries, and peddle reformist delusions that subordinate the working class to the bourgeoisie.
annotation.explanation: Lenin defines Blancism: the historical tendency of moderate socialists to abandon independent class struggle, enter capitalist ministries, and peddle reformist delusions that subordinate the working class to the bourgeoisie.

annotation.targetText: Louis Bonaparte took the political power from the capitalists under the pretext of protecting them
annotation.summary: Bonapartism: state executive power claiming independence while safeguarding capitalist exploitation.
annotation.explanation: Engels analyzes how Bonapartism arises when class struggle produces an equilibrium of weakness: the autocratic state appears to rule above classes while expanding capitalist industry and financial speculation.

annotation.targetText: For the capitalists are well aware that the old type of family, where the woman is a slave and where the husband is responsible for the well-being of his wife and children, constitutes the best weapon to stifle the desire of the working class for freedom. The worker is weighed down by his family cares and is obliged to compromise with capital.
annotation.summary: How the isolated nuclear family serves capitalism: financial anxiety over feeding dependents forces workers to accept wage cuts and suppress revolutionary strikes out of immediate survival fears.
annotation.explanation: How the isolated nuclear family serves capitalism: financial anxiety over feeding dependents forces workers to accept wage cuts and suppress revolutionary strikes out of immediate survival fears.

annotation.targetText: general principles laid down in the Manifesto are, on the whole, as correct today as ever
annotation.summary: Enduring validity of Marxist principles: foundational scientific analysis of class struggle remains intact.
annotation.explanation: Marx and Engels emphasize that while specific tactical demands vary with historical conditions, the core materialist analysis of class struggle, capital accumulation, and historical development remains universally valid.

annotation.targetText: The history of all hitherto existing society(2) is the history of class struggles.
annotation.summary: All recorded history is driven by struggle between oppressor and oppressed classes, not by great individuals or ideas.
annotation.explanation: This is the opening thesis of the Manifesto and the core of historical materialism: freeman and slave, lord and serf, guild-master and journeyman all stood in open or hidden conflict, and each epoch ended either in revolutionary reconstruction of society or in the common ruin of the contending classes.
annotation.context: Marx and Engels did not claim class struggle was a new discovery; they argued that it explains the transitions between modes of production and that capitalism simplifies society into two great camps.

annotation.targetText: What the bourgeoisie therefore produces, above all, are its own grave-diggers. Its fall and the victory of the proletariat are equally inevitable.
annotation.summary: By building large industry and a concentrated working class, capitalism creates the force that will overthrow it.
annotation.explanation: The proletariat is not an outside enemy of capitalism but its own product. Factory production gathers workers together, organises them and teaches them to act collectively, so the growth of capital is simultaneously the growth of its grave-diggers.
annotation.context: Later Marxists such as Lenin and Luxemburg used this passage to argue that organisation and political consciousness, not spontaneous misery alone, turn the working class into a revolutionary force.

annotation.targetText: Law, morality, religion, are to him so many bourgeois prejudices, behind which lurk in ambush just as many bourgeois interests.
annotation.summary: For the modern worker, law, morality and religion are not neutral truths but disguises for the interests of the ruling class.
annotation.explanation: Marx and Engels describe how wage labour strips the worker of illusions: daily experience shows that bourgeois law protects property, bourgeois morality excuses exploitation, and religion often sanctifies the existing order.
annotation.context: This is an early statement of the Marxist theory of ideology, which later became central to analyses of religion and the superstructure.

annotation.targetText: In place of the old bourgeois society, with its classes and class antagonisms, we shall have an association, in which the free development of each is the condition for the free development of all.
annotation.summary: Communist society replaces class antagonism with an association where each person's freedom depends on the freedom of everyone.
annotation.explanation: This sentence states the humanist goal of the whole programme. Abolishing private ownership of the means of production is not an end in itself but the precondition for individual development that is no longer bought at the expense of other classes.
annotation.context: It is frequently cited against the claim that Marxism seeks to submerge the individual in the collective.

annotation.targetText: The working men have no country. We cannot take from them what they have not got.
annotation.summary: Because workers hold no property in the nation, their interests cross borders and nationalism cannot unite them with their own employers.
annotation.explanation: The line answers the charge that communists want to abolish countries. Marx and Engels argue that the working class is already stripped of national character by capitalism and that its political supremacy must first be won inside each nation before it can become international.
annotation.context: The slogan underlies the internationalist position that Lenin later used against social chauvinism during the First World War.

annotation.targetText: But Communism abolishes eternal truths, it abolishes all religion, and all morality, instead of constituting them on a new basis; it therefore acts in contradiction to all past historical experience.
annotation.summary: The charge that communism destroys religion and morality is answered by pointing out that all past ideas were shaped by class antagonism.
annotation.explanation: Marx and Engels turn the accusation around: since all past society moved through class antagonisms, the ideas of every age share common forms. Communism breaks with traditional property relations and therefore with traditional ideas.
annotation.context: This is one of the clearest statements that Marxism treats morality and religion as historical products rather than timeless absolutes.

annotation.targetText: The proletarians have nothing to lose but their chains. They have a world to win.
annotation.summary: The closing call states that workers have no property interest in the present order and everything to gain from overturning it.
annotation.explanation: The ending contrasts the ruling classes trembling at a communist revolution with a working class that risks only its chains. It fuses the open declaration of aims with the demand for the forcible overthrow of existing social conditions.
annotation.context: Combined with the final slogan 'Working Men of All Countries, Unite!', it became the most reproduced line of the socialist movement.

annotation.targetText:
The value of labour-power is determined, as in the case of every
other commodity, by the labour-time necessary for the production, and consequently
also the reproduction, of this special article.
annotation.summary: The value of labor-power: determined by the labor-time necessary for the production and reproduction of the worker's means of subsistence.
annotation.explanation: Wages reflect the cost of reproducing labor-power: the food, housing, training, and healthcare required for the worker to return to work tomorrow and raise children.

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)
annotations.chapterTitle: The Buying and Selling of Labour-Power

annotation.targetText: In order that a man may be able to sell commodities other than labour-power, he must of course have the means of production, as raw material, implements, &c. No boots can be made without leather. He requires also the means of subsistence.
annotation.summary: The separation of producers from the means of production: workers are compelled to sell labour-power because they lack productive property.
annotation.explanation: A person cannot sell products without access to raw materials, tools, and land. When direct producers are dispossessed of their means of production, their only remaining marketable possession is their capacity to work (labour-power).
annotation.context: Part II, Chapter 6: The Buying and Selling of Labour-Power

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)
annotations.chapterTitle: The Buying and Selling of Labour-Power

annotation.targetText: For the conversion of his money into capital, therefore, the owner of money must meet in the market with the free labourer, free in the double sense, that as a free man he can dispose of his labour-power as his own commodity, and that on the other hand he has no other commodity for sale, is short of everything necessary for the realisation of his labour-power.
annotation.summary: The double freedom of the proletarian: free to sell labour-power, and free from any ownership of the means of production.
annotation.explanation: Marx underscores the historical irony of bourgeois "freedom". The proletarian is free in two senses: legally free as an individual to dispose of their labour-power on the market (unlike a feudal serf or slave), and simultaneously free (bereft) of any means of production or subsistence, forcing them to submit to wage labour to avoid starvation.
annotation.context: Part II, Chapter 6: The Buying and Selling of Labour-Power

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)
annotations.chapterTitle: The Buying and Selling of Labour-Power

annotation.targetText: The fact that half a day's labour is necessary to keep the labourer alive during 24 hours, does not in any way prevent him from working a whole day. Therefore, the value of labour-power, and the value which that labour-power creates in the labour-process, are two entirely different magnitudes; and this difference of the two values was what the capitalist had in view, when he was purchasing the labour-power.
annotation.summary: The origin of surplus-value: the difference between the value of labour-power and the new value created by working the full day.
annotation.explanation: Here Marx solves the central riddle of capitalist exploitation. The worker needs only, say, 4 or 6 hours of labour to reproduce the value of daily wages. But the capitalist buys the capacity to work for the whole 8, 10, or 12 hour day. The excess hours constitute unpaid surplus labour, which crystallizes into surplus-value pocketed by the capitalist.
annotation.context: Part III, Chapter 7 (Section 2: The Production of Surplus-Value)

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)
annotations.chapterTitle: The Labour-Process and the Process of Producing Surplus-Value

annotation.targetText: surplus-value bears the same ratio to variable capital, that surplus-labour does to necessary labour, or in other words, the rate of surplus-value, s/v = (surplus labour)/(necessary labour). Both ratios, s/v and (surplus labour)/(necessary labour), express the same thing in different ways; in the one case by reference to materialised, incorporated labour, in the other by reference to living, fluent labour.
annotation.summary: The rate of surplus-value formula: the ratio of surplus-labour to necessary labour expressed in materialised and living form.
annotation.explanation: Marx demonstrates that s/v is identical to the ratio of surplus labour-time to necessary labour-time. Whether measured in monetary value or in living hours worked, this fraction reveals the precise proportion of unpaid labour extracted from the working class.
annotation.context: Part III, Chapter 9: The Rate of Surplus-Value

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)

annotation.targetText:
In the United States of North America, every independent movement
of the workers was paralysed so long as slavery disfigured a part of the
Republic. Labour cannot emancipate itself in the white skin where in the
black it is branded. But out of the death of slavery a new life at once
arose. The first fruit of the Civil War was the eight hours' agitation,
that ran with the seven-leagued boots of the locomotive from the Atlantic
to the Pacific, from New England to California.
annotation.summary: "Labour cannot emancipate itself in the white skin where in the black it is branded": racial oppression paralyzes the entire working class.
annotation.explanation: Marx demonstrates that racial slavery and anti-Black racism divide and paralyze the labor movement. Only with the destruction of chattel slavery in the US Civil War could a united national movement for the eight-hour workday emerge.

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)

annotation.targetText: There is here, therefore, an antinomy, right against right, both equally bearing the seal of the law of exchanges. Between equal rights force decides. Hence is it that in the history of capitalist production, the determination of what is a working-day, presents itself as the result of a struggle, a struggle between collective capital, i.e., the class of capitalists, and collective labour, i.e., the working-class.
annotation.summary: Between equal rights, force decides: class struggle determines the length of the working day.
annotation.explanation: The capitalist asserts the buyer right to extract as much labour as possible; the worker asserts the seller right to protect their health and life. Both rights comply with bourgeois contract law. Therefore, only class struggle and collective social power can settle the boundary of the working day.
annotation.context: Part III, Chapter 10: The Working-Day (Section 1: The Limits of the Working-Day)

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)

annotation.targetText: prolongation of the working day, I call absolute surplus-value. On the other hand, the surplus-value arising from the curtailment of the necessary labour-time, and from the corresponding alteration in the respective lengths of the two components of the working day, I call relative surplus-value.
annotation.summary: Absolute versus relative surplus-value: lengthening the working day versus shortening necessary labour-time.
annotation.explanation: Capital has two methods to expand surplus-value: absolute surplus-value lengthens the total working day (e.g. from 10 to 12 hours); relative surplus-value increases productivity in consumer-goods industries, lowering the cost of workers subsistence and shrinking necessary labour-time without extending total hours.
annotation.context: Part IV, Chapter 12: The Concept of Relative Surplus-Value

annotation.targetText:
Formerly the individual work of a Nuremberg
artificer, the watch has been transformed into the social product of an
immense number of detail labourers
annotation.summary: Under manufacture, each worker performs only one tiny fraction of the total production process. This "detail laborer" becomes extremely skilled at their single task but loses the ability to produce a complete product independently.
annotation.explanation: Under manufacture, each worker performs only one tiny fraction of the total production process. This "detail laborer" becomes extremely skilled at their single task but loses the ability to produce a complete product independently.

annotation.targetText: crippled monstrosity, by forcing his detail dexterity at the expense of a world of productive capabilities and instincts; just as in the States of La Plata they butcher a whole beast for the sake of his hide or his tallow.
annotation.summary: The crippling of human potential: manufacture suppresses all-round creative capacities to boost detail dexterity.
annotation.explanation: Marx passionately critiques how capitalist manufacturing mutilates human faculties. By isolating a single mechanical skill at the expense of general cognitive and physical development, capitalism cripples the worker into an appendage of capital.
annotation.context: Part IV, Chapter 14: Division of Labour and Manufacture

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)

annotation.targetText: John Stuart Mill says in his "Principles of Political Economy": "It is questionable if all the mechanical inventions yet made have lightened the day's toil of any human being." [1] That is, however, by no means the aim of the capitalistic application of machinery. Like every other increase in the productiveness of labour, machinery is intended to cheapen commodities, and, by shortening that portion of the working-day, in which the labourer works for himself, to lengthen the other portion that he gives, without an equivalent, to the capitalist. In short, it is a means for producing surplus-value.
annotation.summary: The capitalist aim of machinery: not to ease human toil, but to cheapen commodities and maximize surplus-value.
annotation.explanation: Refuting liberal technological optimism, Marx shows that under capitalism, machinery is introduced not to lighten human labour or reduce working hours, but to reduce the value of labour-power and maximize the unpaid surplus-value appropriated by capital.
annotation.context: Part IV, Chapter 15: Machinery and Modern Industry (Section 1)

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)

annotation.targetText: In so far as machinery dispenses with muscular power, it becomes a means of employing labourers of slight muscular strength, and those whose bodily development is incomplete, but whose limbs are all the more supple. The labour of women and children was, therefore, the first thing sought for by capitalists who used machinery. That mighty substitute for labour and labourers was forthwith changed into a means for increasing the number of wage-labourers by enrolling, under the direct sway of capital, every member of the workman's family, without distinction of age or sex.
annotation.summary: Subjugation of the whole working family: machinery enables capital to enroll women and child labourers under its direct sway.
annotation.explanation: By replacing physical muscular exertion with automated mechanisms, machinery allows capital to break craft barriers and employ women and children at depressed wage rates, devaluing adult male wages and subjecting the entire working-class household to factory exploitation.
annotation.context: Part IV, Chapter 15: Machinery and Modern Industry (Section 3: The Proximate Effects of Machinery on the Workman)

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)

annotation.targetText: It is the most powerful weapon for repressing strikes, those periodical revolts of the working-class against the autocracy of capital.
annotation.summary: Machinery as a political weapon: technological automation is deployed by capital to smash workers strikes and resistance.
annotation.explanation: New industrial inventions are not politically neutral technical advancements; capital repeatedly introduces machinery specifically to break strikes, bypass skilled trade union resistance, and impose the autocracy of capital upon factory floor discipline.
annotation.context: Part IV, Chapter 15: Machinery and Modern Industry (Section 5: The Strife Between Workman and Machine)

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)

annotation.targetText:
Capitalist production is not merely the production of commodities,
it is essentially the production of surplus-value. The labourer produces,
not for himself, but for capital. It no longer suffices, therefore, that
he should simply produce. He must produce surplus-value. That labourer
alone is productive, who produces surplus-value for the capitalist, and
thus works for the self-expansion of capital.
annotation.summary: Productive labour under capitalism: a worker is productive only if they produce surplus-value for capital.
annotation.explanation: Under capitalism, production exists not merely to create useful goods, but fundamentally to generate surplus value. A worker is "productive" only insofar as they produce profit for their employer.
annotation.context: Part V, Chapter 16: Absolute and Relative Surplus-Value

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)

annotation.targetText: Surplus-value and the value of labour-power vary in opposite directions. A variation in the productiveness of labour, its increase or diminution, causes a variation in the opposite direction in the value of labour-power, and in the same direction in surplus-value.
annotation.summary: Inverse variation of surplus-value and wages: productivity gains in wage goods reduce the value of labour-power and raise surplus-value.
annotation.explanation: When productivity rises in industries producing food, clothing, and shelter, the value of labour-power falls. Consequently, the capitalist extracts a larger proportion of surplus-value even if the real material standard of living of the worker remains unchanged or rises slightly.
annotation.context: Part V, Chapter 17: Changes of Magnitude in the Price of Labour-Power and in Surplus-Value (Section 1)

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)
annotations.chapterTitle: Changes of Magnitude in the Price of Labour-Power and in Surplus-Value

annotation.targetText: The wage form thus extinguishes every trace of the division of the working-day into necessary labour and surplus-labour, into paid and unpaid labour. All labour appears as paid labour. In the corvée, the labour of the worker for himself, and his compulsory labour for his lord, differ in space and time in the clearest possible way. In slave labour, even that part of the working-day in which the slave is only replacing the value of his own means of existence, in which, therefore, in fact, he works for himself alone, appears as labour for his master. All the slave's labour appears as unpaid labour. [8] In wage labour, on the contrary, even surplus-labour, or unpaid labour, appears as paid. There the property-relation conceals the labour of the slave for himself; here the money-relation conceals the unrequited labour of the wage labourer.
annotation.summary: The wage-form obscures exploitation: comparing corvée, chattel slavery, and wage labour.
annotation.explanation: Under feudal corvée, compulsory unpaid labour for the lord is visibly separated in space and time from labour on one own plot. Under slavery, all labour appears unpaid, concealing the time the slave works for their own subsistence. Under wage labour, the money-relation creates the opposite mystification: all labour appears paid, concealing the unpaid surplus labour extracted by the capitalist.
annotation.context: Part VI, Chapter 19: The Transformation of the Value of Labour-Power into Wages

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)
annotations.chapterTitle: The Transformation of the Value (and Respective Price) of Labour-Power into Wages

annotation.targetText: The sum of money [1] which the labourer receives for his daily or weekly labour, forms the amount of his nominal wages, or of his wages estimated in value. But it is clear that according to the length of the working-day, that is, according to the amount of actual labour daily supplied, the same daily or weekly wage may represent very different prices of labour, i.e., very different sums of money for the same quantity of labour.
annotation.summary: Nominal wages versus price of labour: the length of the working day conceals the real rate of exploitation under time-wages.
annotation.explanation: An apparently high weekly paycheck can disguise severe exploitation if the worker is forced to work 12 or 14 hours a day. Under time-wages, the true index of exploitation is not the nominal daily wage, but the hourly price of labour-power.
annotation.context: Part VI, Chapter 20: Time-Wages

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)

annotation.targetText: Given piece-wage, it is naturally the personal interest of the labourer to strain his labour-power as intensely as possible; this enables the capitalist to raise more easily the normal degree of intensity of labour. [8] It is moreover now the personal interest of the labourer to lengthen the working-day, since with it his daily or weekly wages rise.
annotation.summary: Self-intensification of exploitation under piece-wages: workers are driven to lengthen their own working day.
annotation.explanation: Under piece-work, workers are pressured by low rates to intensify their own effort and work excessive overtime. Once high output becomes normal, the capitalist cuts the piece-rate, compelling workers to produce even more units merely to maintain their original income.
annotation.context: Part VI, Chapter 21: Piece-Wages

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)

annotation.targetText: piece-wage is the form of wages most in harmony with the capitalist mode of production. Although by no means new ; it figures side by side with time-wages officially in the French and English labour statutes of the 14th century ; it only conquers a larger field for action during the period of manufacture, properly so-called.
annotation.summary: Piece-wages: the form of wages most in harmony with the capitalist mode of production.
annotation.explanation: Piece-wages convert payment into a piece-rate incentive structure. This form allows capital to dispense with extensive supervisory oversight, since workers discipline themselves to maximize output, while quality control is weaponized to make wage deductions.
annotation.context: Part VI, Chapter 21: Piece-Wages

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)

annotation.targetText: under its aspect of a continuous connected process, of a process of reproduction, produces not only commodities, not only surplus-value, but it also produces and reproduces the capitalist relation; on the one side the capitalist, on the other the wage labourer.
annotation.summary: Reproduction of the capitalist relation: capitalism continuously reproduces both commodities and the unequal class relationship.
annotation.explanation: Capitalist production is not a one-off transaction. As a continuous process of reproduction, it inexorably reproduces the structural class divide: the worker exits the production cycle with nothing but their labour-power to sell again tomorrow, while the capitalist exits with accumulated capital to command labour anew.
annotation.context: Part VII, Chapter 23: Simple Reproduction

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)

annotation.targetText: It forms a disposable industrial reserve army, that belongs to capital quite as absolutely as if the latter had bred it at its own cost. Independently of the limits of the actual increase of population, it creates, for the changing needs of the self-expansion of capital, a mass of human material always ready for exploitation.
annotation.summary: The industrial reserve army: capitalism necessarily creates and requires a pool of unemployed workers to regulate wages and discipline labour.
annotation.explanation: Unemployment is not an accidental market imperfection, but a systemic necessity for capitalist accumulation. The industrial reserve army provides an elastic reservoir of disposable labour that expands during boom times, contracts during crises, and holds down wage demands through competitive desperation.
annotation.context: Part VII, Chapter 25: The General Law of Capitalist Accumulation (Section 3)

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)
annotations.chapterTitle: The General Law of Capitalist Accumulation

annotation.targetText: Accumulation of wealth at one pole is, therefore, at the same time accumulation of misery, agony of toil slavery, ignorance, brutality, mental degradation, at the opposite pole, i.e., on the side of the class that produces its own product in the form of capital.
annotation.summary: The absolute general law of capitalist accumulation: polarization of wealth at one pole and misery, toil, and degradation at the other.
annotation.explanation: Marx formulates the culminating contradiction of capitalist accumulation. The more social wealth and capital expand, the deeper the relative misery, insecurity, and subordination inflicted upon the working class whose collective labour generates that very wealth.
annotation.context: Part VII, Chapter 25: The General Law of Capitalist Accumulation (Section 4)

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)
annotations.chapterTitle: The General Law of Capitalist Accumulation

annotation.targetText: The process, therefore, that clears the way for the capitalist system, can be none other than the process which takes away from the labourer the possession of his means of production; a process that transforms, on the one hand, the social means of subsistence and of production into capital, on the other, the immediate producers into wage labourers. The so-called primitive accumulation, therefore, is nothing else than the historical process of divorcing the producer from the means of production.
annotation.summary: The secret of primitive accumulation: the violent historical divorcing of direct producers from their means of production.
annotation.explanation: Capital did not originate from the thrifty savings of virtuous entrepreneurs, as bourgeois economists pretend. Primitive accumulation was the brutal, violent historical process through which peasants and artisans were forcibly separated from their land and tools, creating both concentrated capital and a propertyless working class.
annotation.context: Part VIII, Chapter 26: The Secret of Primitive Accumulation

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)

annotation.targetText:
In England, serfdom had practically disappeared in the
last part of the 14th century. The immense majority of the
population [1]
consisted then, and to a still larger extent, in the 15th
century, of free peasant proprietors, whatever was the
feudal title under which their right of property was hidden.
annotation.summary: Prior to capitalism, English peasants were largely free proprietors with access to common land rather than wage laborers.
annotation.explanation: Before capitalism, English peasants were largely free proprietors with access to common land. The subsequent enclosure movement violently dispossessed them, creating a landless workforce forced to sell their labor.

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)
annotations.chapterTitle: Expropriation of the Agricultural Population from the Land

annotation.targetText:
The parliamentary form of the robbery is that of Acts for
enclosures of Commons, in other words, decrees by which the
landlords grant themselves the people's land as private
property, decrees of expropriation of the people.
annotation.summary: Parliamentary acts for the enclosure of commons served as the legalized instrument for expropriating peasant communal lands.
annotation.explanation: The state apparatus directly facilitated primitive accumulation by passing enclosure acts, turning common lands that sustained peasant livelihoods into exclusive private property for wealthy landlords.
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)
annotations.chapterTitle: Expropriation of the Agricultural Population from the Land

annotation.targetText:
The spoliation of the church's
property, the fraudulent alienation of the State domains,
the robbery of the common lands, the usurpation of feudal
and clan property, and its transformation into modern
private property under circumstances of reckless terrorism,
were just so many idyllic methods of primitive accumulation.
They conquered the field for capitalistic agriculture, made
the soil part and parcel of capital, and created for the
town industries the necessary supply of a "free" and
outlawed proletariat.
annotation.summary: The violent expropriation of church, state, and communal lands under state-sanctioned terror forged the landless proletariat necessary for capitalist industry.
annotation.explanation: Capitalist production was not born from frugal saving, but from violent, state-backed theft of lands and resources, converting the soil into commercial capital and forcing the population into wage slavery.
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)
annotations.chapterTitle: Expropriation of the Agricultural Population from the Land

annotation.targetText: the whole of the 16th century, throughout Western Europe a bloody legislation against vagabondage. The fathers of the present working class were chastised for their enforced transformation into vagabonds and paupers. Legislation treated them as "voluntary" criminals, and assumed that it depended on their own good will to go on working under the old conditions that no longer existed.
annotation.summary: Bloody legislation against vagabondage: the state criminalizes the dispossessed peasantry to enforce wage labour.
annotation.explanation: Peasants driven from the land could not be absorbed into early manufactures quickly enough. The state stepped in with savage criminal statutes: whipping, branding with hot irons, and enslavement for vagrancy: coercing displaced rural populations into the brutal discipline required by emerging capital.
annotation.context: Part VIII, Chapter 28: Bloody Legislation against the Expropriated
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)
annotations.chapterTitle: Bloody Legislation against the Expropriated, from the End of the 15th Century. Forcing down of Wages by Acts of Parliament

annotation.targetText: The bourgeoisie, at its rise, wants and uses the power of the state to "regulate" wages, i.e., to force them within the limits suitable for surplus-value making, to lengthen the working-day and to keep the labourer himself in the normal degree of dependence. This is an essential element of the so-called primitive accumulation.
annotation.summary: State regulation of wages: the rising bourgeoisie deploys state power to cap wages and prolong the working day.
annotation.explanation: Far from believing in free-market wage setting, the early capitalist class relied on state legislation to impose wage ceilings and penalize workers who demanded higher pay, ensuring a high rate of surplus-value extraction.
annotation.context: Part VIII, Chapter 28: Bloody Legislation against the Expropriated
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)
annotations.chapterTitle: Bloody Legislation against the Expropriated, from the End of the 15th Century. Forcing down of Wages by Acts of Parliament

annotation.targetText: recious metals, and therefore of money, brought the farmers golden fruit. Apart from all the other circumstances discussed above, it lowered wages. A portion of the latter was now added to the profits of the farm. The continuous rise in the price of corn, wool, meat, in a word of all agricultural produce, swelled the money capital of the farmer without any action on his part, whilst the rent he paid (being calculated on the old value of money) diminished in reality.
annotation.summary: The enrichment of the capitalist farmer: inflation and depreciating money enrich agricultural capitalists at the expense of workers and landlords.
annotation.explanation: During the 16th-century price revolution, the influx of American precious metals depreciated currency. Long-term agricultural leases remained fixed in depreciated money, while crop prices soared and real wages fell, allowing capitalist tenant farmers to amass substantial capital from the twin exploitation of agricultural labourers and landlords.
annotation.context: Part VIII, Chapter 29: Genesis of the Capitalist Farmer

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)

annotation.targetText:
The discovery of gold and silver in America, the extirpation,
enslavement and entombment in mines of the aboriginal population, the beginning
of the conquest and looting of the East Indies, the turning of Africa into
a warren for the commercial hunting of black-skins, signalised the rosy
dawn of the era of capitalist production. These idyllic proceedings are
the chief momenta of primitive accumulation.
annotation.summary: The birth of capitalism ("primitive accumulation") was built directly on Indigenous genocide, colonial plunder, and the transatlantic slave trade.
annotation.explanation: Marx refutes the bourgeois myth that capitalism arose from peaceful thrift, showing that European industrial wealth was accumulated through Indigenous dispossession in the Americas, colonial looting in India, and the enslavement of Africans.

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)

annotation.targetText: The capitalist mode of appropriation, the result of the capitalist mode of production, produces capitalist private property. This is the first negation of individual private property, as founded on the labour of the proprietor. But capitalist production begets, with the inexorability of a law of Nature, its own negation. It is the negation of negation. This does not re-establish private property for the producer, but gives him individual property based on the acquisition of the capitalist era: i.e., on cooperation and the possession in common of the land and of the means of production.
annotation.summary: The negation of negation: capitalist socialization culminates in the expropriation of private property in favor of common ownership.
annotation.explanation: Individual private property based on self-earned labour was first negated by capitalist private property (the expropriation of many small producers by few capitalists). In turn, capitalist development inexorably socializes the labour process, leading to the negation of negation: the collective appropriation of the means of production by the associated working class.
annotation.context: Part VIII, Chapter 32: Historical Tendency of Capitalist Accumulation

annotations.bookTitle: Capital: Volume 1 (The Process of Production of Capital)

annotation.targetText: The first contradiction is the contradiction between labour and capital. Imperialism is the omnipotence of the monopolist trusts and syndicates, of the banks and the financial oligarchy, in the industrial countries. In the fight against this omnipotence, the customary methods of the working class: trade unions and cooperatives, parliamentary parties and the parliamentary struggle: have proved to be totally inadequate. Either place yourself at the mercy of capital, eke out a wretched existence as of old and sink lower and lower, or adopt a new weapon: this is the alternative imperialism puts before the vast masses of the proletariat. Imperialism brings the working class to revolution.
annotation.summary: Imperialist monopoly capital intensifies class exploitation beyond the capacity of legal trade unionism.
annotation.explanation: Under monopoly capitalism, the financial oligarchy and giant corporate syndicates concentrate economic power to an extreme degree. Peaceful, reformist parliamentary methods and legal trade union negotiations become completely inadequate to defend working-class survival, leaving socialist revolution as the only viable path forward.

annotations.chapterTitle: I. The Historical Roots of Leninism

annotation.targetText: The fundamental question of Leninism, its point of departure, is not the peasant question, but the question of the dictatorship of the proletariat, of the conditions under which it can be achieved, of the conditions under which it can be consolidated. The peasant question, as the question of the ally of the proletariat in its struggle for power, is a derivative question.
annotation.summary: The peasant question is the question of the strategic ally of the proletariat in the struggle for power.
annotation.explanation: The fundamental objective of Leninism is the proletarian dictatorship. The peasant question is vital as a derivative of that goal: without the revolutionary alliance between industrial workers and working peasants, the proletariat cannot successfully seize or retain state power.
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotation.targetText: Strategy is the determination of the direction of the main blow of the proletariat at a given stage of the revolution, the elaboration of a corresponding plan for the disposition of the revolutionary forces (main and secondary reserves), the fight to carry out this plan throughout the given stage of the revolution.
annotation.summary: Strategy determines the direction of the main blow of the proletariat across a historic revolutionary stage.
annotation.explanation: Defines strategy as the overarching plan for aligning class forces, selecting principal and secondary reserves, and directing mass energy toward decisive political objectives at each historical phase of the revolutionary struggle.

annotation.targetText:
In the present historical conditions of Latin America, the national
bourgeoisie cannot lead the ant feudal and anti-imperialist struggle.
Experience demonstrates that in our nations this class : even when
its interests clash with those of Yankee imperialism : has been
incapable of confronting imperialism, paralyzed by fear of social
revolution and frightened by the clamor of the exploited masses.
annotation.summary: The Latin American national bourgeoisie cannot lead anti-imperialist liberation because fear of the working masses binds it to imperialism.
annotation.explanation: Unlike the progressive European bourgeoisie of the 18th century, the dependent capitalist classes of the Global South are deeply intertwined with landed oligarchs and foreign imperialist capital. Terrified of popular social revolution from below, the national bourgeoisie inevitably capitulates to imperialism rather than leading genuine national emancipation.
annotation.context: Written in the context of the Alliance for Progress and reformist illusions among Latin American bourgeois parties in the early 1960s.

annotation.targetText:
One ought to be "Marxist' with the same naturalness with which
one is "Newtonian" in physics, or "Pasteurian" in
biology
annotation.summary: Che rejects dogmatic sectarianism by comparing Marxism to established natural sciences. Just as modern physics builds upon Newton's discovered laws of mechanics, revolutionary social science builds upon Marx's discovered laws of class struggle and historical materialism.
annotation.explanation: Che rejects dogmatic sectarianism by comparing Marxism to established natural sciences. Just as modern physics builds upon Newton's discovered laws of mechanics, revolutionary social science builds upon Marx's discovered laws of class struggle and historical materialism.

annotations.bookTitle: Notes for the Study of the Ideology of the Cuban Revolution
annotations.chapterTitle: Notes for the Study of the Ideology of the Cuban Revolution

annotation.targetText: There is no doubt that the development is going in the direction of a single world trust that will swallow up all enterprises and all states without exception. But the development in this direction is proceeding under such stress, with such a tempo, with such contradictions, conflicts, and convulsions-not only economical, but also political, national, etc., etc.-that before a single world trust will be reached, before the respective national finance capitals will have formed a world union of "ultra-imperialism," imperialism will inevitably explode, capitalism will turn into its opposite.
annotation.summary: Before global capitalism could ever unite into Kautsky's peaceful 'single world trust', its violent contradictions will cause imperialism to explode in socialist revolution.
annotation.explanation: Lenin refutes Karl Kautsky's reformist dream of 'ultra-imperialism', demonstrating that the uneven, catastrophic development of monopoly capitalism intensifies wars and class struggles long before a global monopoly could peacefully consolidate.

annotation.targetText: It is perfectly obvious that not races but state organisations of definite groups of the bourgeoisie are conducting the struggle. It is also perfectly obvious that one or the other grouping of the great powers is determined, not by a community of certain racial tasks, but by a community of capitalist aims at a given moment.
annotation.summary: Bukharin demolishes racial theories of imperialism, showing that military alliances follow capitalist profit interests rather than racial identity.
annotation.explanation: Pointing to multi-ethnic war coalitions and shifting alliances among European and Asian powers, Bukharin exposes racial ideology as a ruling-class fabrication designed to mask the war aims of finance capital.

annotations.chapterTitle: Ch. IX: Imperialism as an Historic Category

annotation.targetText: Marxism teaches us that the historic process, and consequently every link in the chain of historic events, is a "necessary" entity. To deduce political fatalism from this doctrine is absurd, for the simple reason that historic events are taking place not outside of but through the will of people, through the class struggle if we deal with a class society.
annotation.summary: Historical necessity does not mean passive fatalism; history operates through conscious human agency and the class struggle.
annotation.explanation: Bukharin refutes both bourgeois caricatures of 'fatalist Marxism' and Kautsky's opportunist passivity, showing that recognizing the historical necessity of imperialism guides active revolutionary struggle against it.

annotation.targetText: For the collapse of the proletarian movement is a result of the unequal situation of the "state capitalist trusts" within the boundaries of world economy. Just as it is impossible to understand modern capitalism and its imperialist policy without analysing the tendencies of world capitalism, so the basic tendencies in the proletarian movement cannot be understood without analysing world capitalism.
annotation.summary: The 1914 betrayal of the Second International stemmed from the privileged position of imperialist state-capitalist trusts in the world economy.
annotation.explanation: Bukharin shows how superprofits from colonial exploitation allowed metropolitan capitalists to cultivate a reformist labor aristocracy that temporarily identified its interests with its own imperialist state.

annotations.chapterTitle: Ch. XIV: World Economy and Proletarian Socialism

annotation.targetText: To recognise defence of the fatherland means recognising the legitimacy and justice of war. Legitimacy and justice from what point of view? Only from the point of view of the socialist, proletariat and its struggle for its emancipation. We do not recognise any other point of view. If war is waged by the exploiting class with the object of strengthening its rule as a class, such a war is a criminal war, and “defencism” in such a war is a base betrayal of socialism. If war is waged by the proletariat after it has conquered the bourgeoisie in its own country, and is waged with the object of strengthening and developing socialism, such a war is legitimate and “holy”.
annotation.summary: Marxism judges the justice of a war not by abstract moral formulas, but by which class wages it and for what historical aim.
annotation.explanation: While defending a capitalist nation in an imperialist war is a betrayal of the working class, defending a socialist republic where workers have overthrown the bourgeoisie is a legitimate internationalist duty.
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotations.chapterTitle: II. Proletarian Defencism and Revolutionary Phrase-Making

annotation.targetText: It is in the interest of capital to destroy its enemy (the revolutionary proletariat) bit by bit, before the workers in all countries have united (actually united, i.e., by beginning the revolution). It is in our interest to do all that is possible, to take advantage of the slightest opportunity to postpone the decisive battle until the moment (or until after the moment) the revolutionary workers’ contingents have united in a single great international army.
annotation.summary: Strategic retreat and playing for time protect an isolated socialist revolution from being crushed piecemeal by international capital.
annotation.explanation: Lenin shows that genuine proletarian internationalism requires preserving the existing bastion of socialist power until revolutionary movements in other countries mature.

annotations.chapterTitle: II. Proletarian Defencism and Revolutionary Phrase-Making

annotation.targetText: It is not state capitalism that is at war with socialism, but the petty bourgeoisie plus private capitalism fighting together against both state capitalism and socialism. The petty bourgeoisie oppose every kind of state interference, accounting and control, whether it be state capitalist or state socialist. This is an absolutely unquestionable fact of reality, and the root of the economic mistake of the “Left Communists” is that they have failed to understand it.
annotation.summary: In a predominantly small-peasant economy, the primary internal threat to socialism is petty-bourgeois profiteering and resistance to state accounting, not state capitalism.
annotation.explanation: By attacking 'state capitalism' in 1918, the Left Communists inadvertently aided small-proprietor grain speculators and private black-marketeers who opposed all state regulation and accounting.

annotations.chapterTitle: III. State Capitalism and the Transition to Socialism

annotation.targetText: This should unite all workers who follow the slogan: ‘Get out of the trade unions!’ It is here that the militant proletariat musters its ranks for battle.
annotation.summary: Lenin refutes the ultra-left slogan 'Get out of the trade unions!' as sectarian isolation from the working masses.
annotation.explanation: Lenin refutes ultra-leftists who wanted to abandon conservative trade unions. Revolutionaries must work inside flawed mass institutions where real workers are located.

annotation.explanation: Lenin refutes ultra-leftists who wanted to abandon conservative trade unions. Revolutionaries must work inside flawed mass institutions where real workers are located.

annotation.targetText: In Petrograd, here in Moscow, in other towns and industrial centres the women workers acted splendidly during the revolution. Without them we should not have been victorious.
annotation.summary: Working-class women were indispensable to the victory and defense of the 1917 Bolshevik Revolution.
annotation.explanation: Lenin highlights that proletarian women in Russia bore extreme material deprivation and fought on the front lines of the revolution, proving their central role in working-class victory.

annotation.targetText: The great social question appears as an adjunct, a part, of sexual problems. The main thing becomes a subsidiary matter. That not only endangers clarity on that question itself, it muddles the thoughts, the class-consciousness of proletarian women generally.
annotation.summary: Treating class struggle as secondary to personal sexual theories confuses working-class consciousness.
annotation.explanation: Lenin warns that isolating sex and marriage from the struggle against capitalist exploitation inverts Marxist priorities and weakens revolutionary focus during acute political crises.

annotation.targetText: Our demands are practical conclusions which we have drawn from the burning needs, the shameful humiliation of women, in bourgeois society, defenceless and without rights.

annotation.targetText: The Marxist philosophy of dialectical materialism has two outstanding characteristics. One is its class nature: it openly avows that dialectical materialism is in the service of the proletariat. The other is its practicality: it emphasizes the dependence of theory on practice, emphasizes that theory is based on practice and in turn serves practice.
annotation.summary: Marxist dialectical materialism is defined by two core features: its open class allegiance to the working class, and its practical foundation where theory arises from and guides practice.
annotation.explanation: Unlike bourgeois academic philosophy, which pretends to stand neutrally above classes while defending capitalist social relations, Marxist dialectical materialism openly declares its partisan class standpoint on behalf of the working class and insists that philosophical truth is measured by its practical capacity to emancipate humanity.
annotation.context: Western Neo-Marxist academic departments deliberately severed Marxist theory from working-class political organization, turning it into neutral university seminar commentary divorced from practical struggle.

annotation.explanation: Mao identifies five major operational errors committed by the Japanese command (piecemeal reinforcement, no main direction of attack, lack of coordination, missed opportunities, and failure to annihilate), tracing them to Japan's class contradictions and troop shortages.

annotation.explanation: Mao introduces his central theoretical innovation for socialist governance: separating hostile class antagonisms against counter-revolutionaries from internal disagreements and structural tensions among the working masses and their allies.

annotation.targetText: Fascism is the concentrated expression of the general offensive undertaken by the world bourgeoisie against the proletariat. Its overthrow is therefore an absolute necessity, nay, it is even a question of the every-day existence and of the bread and butter of every ordinary worker.
annotation.summary: Fascism is the concentrated offensive of big capital against the working class and its daily survival.
annotation.explanation: Zetkin establishes that fascism is not an isolated political aberration, but the generalized offensive of the capitalist ruling class to crush working-class living standards and organizations.

annotation.targetText: Fascism, on the contrary, viewed objectively, is not the revenge of the bourgeoisie in retaliation for proletarian aggression against the bourgeoisie, but it is a punishment of the proletariat for failing to carry on the revolution begun in Russia. The Fascist leaders are not a small and exclusive caste; they extend deeply into wide elements of the population.
annotation.summary: Unlike a narrow military junta, fascism is a mass movement that punishes the working class for an uncompleted socialist revolution.
annotation.explanation: Contrasting Mussolini's movement with Admiral Horthy's officer clique in Hungary, Zetkin explains that fascism builds a broad social base among displaced layers of society when reformist betrayal stalls proletarian revolution.

annotation.targetText: Fascism has diverse characteristics in different countries. Nevertheless it has two distinguishing features in all countries, namely, the pretence of a revolutionary programme, which is cleverly adapted to the interests and demands of the large masses, and, on the other hand, the application of the most brutal violence.
annotation.summary: The dual weapon of fascism everywhere: pseudo-revolutionary anti-capitalist demagogy combined with brutal anti-worker terror.
annotation.explanation: Zetkin identifies the universal formula of fascism: it wins mass support by mimicking anti-elitist, revolutionary slogans appealing to ruined lower classes, while deploying paramilitary terror squads against organized labor.
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotation.targetText: The Fascist Party created a double-edged weapon for the corruption and terrorisation of the working class. For the corruption of the working class the Fascist Trade Unions were created, the so-called corporations in which workers and employers were united. To terrorise the working class, the Fascist Party created the militant squads which had grown out of the punitive expeditions.
annotation.summary: Fascist corporatism corrupts labor through class-collaborationist unions while Blackshirt squads terrorize independent workers.
annotation.explanation: In Italy, Mussolini paired Yellow "corporations" (uniting bosses and workers to suppress strikes) with armed paramilitary squads funded by industrialists and landlords to smash revolutionary unions.

annotation.targetText: The proletariat must have a well organised apparatus of self-defence. Whenever Fascism uses violence, it must be met with proletarian violence. I do not mean by this individual terrorist acts, but the violence of the organised revolutionary class struggle of the proletariat. Germany has made a beginning by organising factory "hundreds." This struggle can only be successful if there is a proletarian united front. The workers must unite for this struggle regardless of party.
annotation.summary: Defeating fascism requires a Proletarian United Front across party lines and organized armed working-class self-defense.
annotation.explanation: Rejecting both passive parliamentary appeals and isolated individual terrorism, Zetkin calls for an all-worker United Front and organized workplace defense squads (factory "hundreds") to crush fascist paramilitaries and overthrow capitalism.

annotation.targetText: But it is not a state organisation; nor is it one designed for coercion, but for education. It is an organisation designed to draw in and to train; it is, in fact, a school: a school of administration, a school of economic management, a school of communism.
annotation.summary: Lenin defines the trade union under the dictatorship of the proletariat as an educational institution rather than a coercive state body, designed to train workers in management and cultivate communist consciousness.
annotation.explanation: Lenin defines the trade union under the dictatorship of the proletariat as an educational institution rather than a coercive state body, designed to train workers in management and cultivate communist consciousness.

annotation.targetText: To bring political knowledge to the workers the Social Democrats must go among all classes of the population; they must dispatch units of their army in all directions.
annotation.summary: Socialists must carry political agitation to every class and not confine themselves to economic disputes at the factory.
annotation.explanation: Lenin rejects the idea that workers learn politics only from their own employers. Class political consciousness comes from knowing the relations between all classes and the state, so the party must send its forces among every social stratum.

annotation.targetText: The tide rises and undermines the foundation of state and society. Every one feels that the pillars are swaying and that only powerful props can support them.
annotation.summary: Outlining the necessity of the social revolution, Bebel shows that when capitalist private property becomes an intolerable fetter on socialized production, the organized working class must conquer political power and expropriate the means of production on behalf of society as a whole.
annotation.explanation: Outlining the necessity of the social revolution, Bebel shows that when capitalist private property becomes an intolerable fetter on socialized production, the organized working class must conquer political power and expropriate the means of production on behalf of society as a whole.

annotation.targetText: As soon as society has become the owner of all means of production, the duty to work of all able-bodied persons, regardless of sex, becomes a fundamental law of socialized society.
annotation.summary: In the first chapter of 'The Socialisation of Society', Bebel outlines the fundamental laws of socialist society: the universal duty of all able-bodied persons to work, democratic workplace administration, the replacement of money and commodity trade with labor certificates, and the drastic reduction of the working day through advanced technology and the abolition of parasitic labor.

annotations.chapterTitle: Ch. XXI: Fundamental Laws of Socialistic Society

annotation.targetText: Land, being the prime raw material for all human labor and the basis of human existence, must be made the property of society, together with the means of production and distribution.
annotation.summary: Bebel describes how socialist society will socialize land ownership, apply large-scale scientific agronomy, electric machinery, irrigation, and soil chemistry to agriculture, and abolish the historical antagonism between town and country through decentralized garden communities.
annotation.explanation: Bebel describes how socialist society will socialize land ownership, apply large-scale scientific agronomy, electric machinery, irrigation, and soil chemistry to agriculture, and abolish the historical antagonism between town and country through decentralized garden communities.

annotation.targetText: The late member of the German diet, Dr. Lasker, delivered a lecture in Berlin, during the seventies, in which he arrived at the conclusion that it is possible for all members of society to have an equal standard of education.
annotation.summary: Describing the socialist education system, Bebel envisions universal, secular, co-educational schooling that combines physical development, scientific instruction, and practical polytechnical training from early childhood, freeing parents from financial burdens.
annotation.explanation: Describing the socialist education system, Bebel envisions universal, secular, co-educational schooling that combines physical development, scientific instruction, and practical polytechnical training from early childhood, freeing parents from financial burdens.

annotation.explanation: Bebel depicts everyday life in socialist society: public kitchens, mechanized central laundries, and communal dining halls liberate women from household drudgery, enabling complete individual freedom, travel, intellectual growth, and harmonious social life.
