annotations.chapterTitle: VI. THE PLACE OF ANTAGONISM IN CONTRADICTION

annotation.targetText:
Contradiction and struggle are universal and absolute,
but the methods of resolving contradictions, that is, the forms of struggle,
differ according to the differences in the nature of the contradictions.
annotation.summary: Because conflicts vary in nature, your method of solving them must fit the situation. Real-life example: Differences of opinion among project teammates are resolved through discussion, while structural wage theft requires collective union action or legal pressure.
annotation.explanation: Because conflicts vary in nature, your method of solving them must fit the situation. Real-life example: Differences of opinion among project teammates are resolved through discussion, while structural wage theft requires collective union action or legal pressure.

annotations.chapterTitle: VI. THE PLACE OF ANTAGONISM IN CONTRADICTION

annotation.targetText:
Lenin said, "Antagonism and contradiction are not at all one and the same.
Under socialism, the first will disappear, the second will remain."
annotation.summary: Lenin points out that even in a fair society without exploitation, people will still face challenges, decisions, and debates that drive progress. Real-life example: Even in a close-knit family, members will disagree on house design or budgeting, but those problems are solved through discussion rather than hostility.
annotation.explanation: Lenin points out that even in a fair society without exploitation, people will still face challenges, decisions, and debates that drive progress. Real-life example: Even in a close-knit family, members will disagree on house design or budgeting, but those problems are solved through discussion rather than hostility.

annotations.chapterTitle: VI. THE PLACE OF ANTAGONISM IN CONTRADICTION

annotation.targetText:
The law of contradiction in things,
that is, the law of the unity of opposites, is the fundamental law of nature
and of society and therefore also the fundamental law of thought.
annotation.summary: Mao summarizes that opposing forces drive everything: physical forces in nature, human history, and thoughts in our minds. Real-life example: Understanding this helps us stay calm during big life changes, knowing that tension and conflict are normal parts of growth.
annotation.explanation: Mao summarizes that opposing forces drive everything: physical forces in nature, human history, and thoughts in our minds. Real-life example: Understanding this helps us stay calm during big life changes, knowing that tension and conflict are normal parts of growth.

annotation.targetText:
In studying the particularity and relativity
of contradiction, we must give attention to the distinction between the principal
contradiction and the non-principal contradictions and to the distinction
between the principal aspect and the non-principal aspect of a contradiction
annotation.summary: Solving real-world problems requires separating the main issue from side issues, and recognizing which force holds power right now. Real-life example: A manager who focuses on office decorations while sales drop is failing to separate principal from non-principal issues.
annotation.explanation: Solving real-world problems requires separating the main issue from side issues, and recognizing which force holds power right now. Real-life example: A manager who focuses on office decorations while sales drop is failing to separate principal from non-principal issues.

annotation.targetText:
If, through study, we
achieve a real understanding of the essentials explained above, we shall
be able to demolish dogmatist ideas which are contrary to the basic principles
of Marxism-Leninism and detrimental to our revolutionary cause
annotation.summary: The point of philosophy is practical: replacing rigid, outdated rules with real-world observation. Real-life example: Instead of sticking to an old plan that is failing, a smart leader analyzes current facts and adjusts their strategy to fit reality.
annotation.explanation: The point of philosophy is practical: replacing rigid, outdated rules with real-world observation. Real-life example: Instead of sticking to an old plan that is failing, a smart leader analyzes current facts and adjusts their strategy to fit reality.

annotation.targetText: The Marxist philosophy of dialectical materialism has two outstanding characteristics. One is its class nature: it openly avows that dialectical materialism is in the service of the proletariat. The other is its practicality: it emphasizes the dependence of theory on practice, emphasizes that theory is based on practice and in turn serves practice.
annotation.summary: Marxist dialectical materialism is defined by two core features: its open class allegiance to the working class, and its practical foundation where theory arises from and guides practice.
annotation.explanation: Unlike bourgeois academic philosophy, which pretends to stand neutrally above classes while defending capitalist social relations, Marxist dialectical materialism openly declares its partisan class standpoint on behalf of the working class and insists that philosophical truth is measured by its practical capacity to emancipate humanity.
annotation.context: Western Neo-Marxist academic departments deliberately severed Marxist theory from working-class political organization, turning it into neutral university seminar commentary divorced from practical struggle.

annotations.chapterTitle: On the Relation Between Knowledge and Practice, Between Knowing and Doing

annotation.targetText: If you want knowledge, you must take part in the practice of changing reality. If you want to know the taste of a pear, you must change the pear by eating it yourself.
annotation.summary: Genuine knowledge cannot be gained by passive observation; you can only discover the true nature of reality by actively participating in changing it.
annotation.explanation: Using one of his most famous everyday metaphors, Mao illustrates the materialist principle that genuine knowledge cannot be gained through passive contemplation or armchair speculation; one can only uncover the internal properties and laws of an object by actively interacting with and transforming it.
annotation.context: Labor organizers cannot understand the concrete contradictions of a workplace merely by reading sociological reports; they uncover the real power dynamics only by organizing alongside workers on the shop floor.

annotations.chapterTitle: On the Relation Between Knowledge and Practice, Between Knowing and Doing

annotation.targetText: Anyone who thinks that rational knowledge need not be derived from perceptual knowledge is an idealist. In the history of philosophy there is the "rationalist" school that admits the reality only of reason and not of experience, believing that reason alone is reliable while perceptual experience is not; this school errs by turning things upside down.
annotation.summary: Theories and rational concepts do not drop from the sky; they must be grounded in direct practical experience and concrete investigation, or else they fall into philosophical idealism.
annotation.explanation: Mao critiques philosophical idealism and dogmatic rationalism for treating abstract concepts as self-generated truths independent of material sense experience. Without concrete investigation of material conditions, abstract theories become 'water without a source, a tree without roots.'
annotation.context: Dogmatic sectarians who attempt to apply memorized formulas from another century without investigating current economic data or working-class conditions fall into idealist rationalism.

annotations.chapterTitle: On the Relation Between Knowledge and Practice, Between Knowing and Doing

annotation.targetText: We are also opposed to "Left" phrase-mongering. The thinking of "Leftists" outstrips a given stage of development of the objective process; some regard their fantasies as truth, while others strain to realize in the present an ideal which can only be realized in the future. They alienate themselves from the current practice of the majority of the people and from the realities of the day, and show themselves adventurist in their actions.
annotation.summary: Ultra-leftism detaches revolutionary desires from current material conditions and mass consciousness, mistaking wishful fantasies for immediate reality and leading to reckless adventurism.
annotation.explanation: Mao provides a sharp epistemological diagnosis of ultra-leftism: whereas Right opportunists lag behind objective reality, ultra-leftists detach their subjective desires from the actual material stage of development and the consciousness of the masses, substituting revolutionary-sounding slogans and reckless adventurism for patient mass organization.
annotation.context: Small ultra-left sects that reject united-front coalitions or trade union struggles because those struggles do not immediately abolish capitalism isolate themselves from the working class.

annotations.chapterTitle: On the Relation Between Knowledge and Practice, Between Knowing and Doing

annotation.targetText: Discover the truth through practice, and again through practice verify and develop the truth. Start from perceptual knowledge and actively develop it into rational knowledge; then start from rational knowledge and actively guide revolutionary practice to change both the subjective and the objective world. Practice, knowledge, again practice, and again knowledge.
annotation.summary: Human knowledge develops in an endless upward spiral: starting from practical experience, rising to rational theory, and returning to revolutionary practice to test and deepen truth.
annotation.explanation: Mao's concluding synthesis encapsulates the entire Marxist-Leninist theory of knowledge. Truth is not a static dogma achieved once and for all, but a continuous, upward-spiraling cycle in which practical struggle generates theoretical insight, and theoretical insight guides higher levels of revolutionary practice.
annotation.context: In socialist economic planning and community organizing, policies are formulated from concrete surveys, tested in pilot programs, evaluated against real-world outcomes, and refined for broader implementation.

annotations.chapterTitle: On the Relation Between Knowledge and Practice, Between Knowing and Doing

annotation.targetText: All the experience of the ten months of war proves the error both of the theory of China's inevitable subjugation and of the theory of China's quick victory. The former gives rise to the tendency to compromise and the latter to the tendency to underestimate the enemy. Both approaches to the problem are subjective and one-sided, or, in a word, unscientific.
annotation.summary: Both the belief that China is doomed to lose and the belief that China will win quickly are unscientific errors that focus on only one side of reality.
annotation.explanation: Mao applies materialist dialectics to critique two opposite forms of subjectivism: capitulationist pessimism, which sees only Japan's military strength, and rash optimism, which ignores China's material weaknesses after isolated tactical victories.
annotation.context: In any long liberation or labor struggle, exaggerating the opponent's power leads to surrender, while underestimating their resources after a single win leads to reckless defeat.

annotation.targetText: Thus it can be seen that Japan has great military, economic and political-organizational power, but that her war is reactionary and barbarous, her manpower and material resources are inadequate, and she is in an unfavourable position internationally. China, on the contrary, has less military, economic and political-organizational power, but she is in her era of progress, her war is progressive and just, she is moreover a big country, a factor which enables her to sustain a protracted war, and she will be supported by most countries.
annotation.summary: Japan is militarily strong today, but its war is unjust, its resources are limited, and it is isolated abroad; China is militarily weak today, but its cause is just, its territory and population are vast, and the world supports its struggle.
annotation.explanation: Rather than comparing weapon counts in isolation, Mao analyzes the totality of political, economic, geographic, and international contradictions governing both belligerents, proving why China cannot win quickly but cannot be defeated.
annotation.context: This dialectical framework later explained how anti-colonial movements in Vietnam and Algeria defeated wealthier, heavily armed imperialist powers.

annotation.targetText: Our enemy, Japan, is first of all a moribund imperialist power; she is already in her era of decline and is not only different from Britain at the time of the subjugation of India, when British capitalism was still in the era of its ascendancy, but also different from what she herself was at the time of World War I twenty years ago.
annotation.summary: Japan cannot repeat Britain's past conquest of India because world imperialism is now in decline while China has a Communist Party, a revolutionary army, and global support.
annotation.explanation: Mao shows why mechanical historical analogies fail: whether a small power can conquer a large country depends on the concrete historical epoch, and 1930s fascist imperialism is in its death throes while anti-colonial revolution is rising.
annotation.context: Defeatists often point to past colonial conquests while ignoring how mass political consciousness and international solidarity have transformed the balance of power.

annotations.chapterTitle: Refutation of the Theory of National Subjugation

annotation.targetText: But we are in the midst of a revolutionary war, and revolutionary war is an antitoxin which not only eliminates the enemy's poison but also purges us of our own filth. Every just, revolutionary war is endowed with tremendous power, which can transform many things or clear the way for their transformation.
annotation.summary: A just revolutionary war acts like an antitoxin: it not only defeats the foreign invader, but also cleanses society of internal corruption and backwardness.
annotation.explanation: Mao highlights how the practical necessities of a just war of national liberation force democratic reforms, mass organization, and the exposure of corrupt bureaucrats, accelerating social transformation.
annotation.context: Throughout the anti-Japanese war, areas organized around popular resistance abolished feudal abuses, expanded literacy, and empowered peasant associations.

annotations.chapterTitle: Compromise or Resistance? Corruption or Progress?

annotation.targetText: Do we deny the danger of national subjugation? No, we do not. We recognize that China faces two possible prospects, liberation or subjugation, and that the two are in violent conflict. Our task is to achieve liberation and to avert subjugation.
annotation.summary: Dialectical analysis neither ignores the real danger of defeat nor treats defeat as inevitable; instead, it identifies the concrete conditions needed to turn the possibility of liberation into reality.
annotation.explanation: Mao contrasts materialist dialectics with both fatalistic pessimism and blind optimism: both liberation and subjugation exist as competing possibilities, and conscious struggle determines which side prevails.
annotation.context: Unlike Kuomintang defeatists who saw only China's weaknesses or rash optimists who ignored them, the Communist Party analyzed how to actively build the conditions for victory.

annotations.chapterTitle: The Theory of National Subjugation Is Wrong and the Theory of Quick Victory Is Likewise Wrong

annotation.targetText: The enemy is strong and we are weak, and the danger of subjugation is there. But in other respects the enemy has shortcomings and we have advantages. The enemy's advantage can be reduced and his shortcomings aggravated by our efforts. On the other hand, our advantages can be enhanced and our shortcoming remedied by our efforts.
annotation.summary: Because strength and weakness are relative rather than fixed, sustained struggle can wear down the enemy's initial military advantage while multiplying the people's political and geographic advantages.
annotation.explanation: Mao explains why the war must be protracted: it takes time and persistent effort to erode Japan's military superiority and develop China's latent advantages to the point where the balance of power flips.
annotation.context: Even while Western corporations continued selling war materials to Japan in 1938, prolonged Chinese resistance steadily drained Japan's finances and manpower.

annotation.targetText: The first stage covers the period of the enemy's strategic offensive and our strategic defensive. The second stage will be the period of the enemy's strategic consolidation and our preparation for the counter-offensive. The third stage will be the period of our strategic counter-offensive and the enemy's strategic retreat.
annotation.summary: The protracted war unfolds in three stages: defending against the enemy's initial offensive, wearing the enemy down during a long stalemate, and launching the final counter-offensive.
annotation.explanation: Mao maps the dialectical transformation of the war from strategic defensive through prolonged stalemate to strategic counter-offensive, explaining how guerrilla and mobile warfare gradually shift China from inferiority to parity and finally superiority.
annotation.context: The Sino-Japanese War from 1937 to 1945 followed this exact trajectory: rapid Japanese advances into 1938, a prolonged stalemate with vast rural guerrilla bases from 1939 to 1944, and the final counter-offensive in 1945.

annotations.chapterTitle: The Three Stages of the Protracted War

annotation.targetText: Thus there are two forms of encirclement by the enemy forces and two forms of encirclement by our own: rather like a game of weichi. [16] Campaigns and battles fought by the two sides resemble the capturing of each other's pieces, and the establishment of enemy strongholds (such as Talyuan) and our guerrilla base areas (such as the Wutai Mountains) resembles moves to dominate spaces on the board.
annotation.summary: Although Japan surrounds China strategically, China's rural guerrilla bases surround Japan's occupied cities and railways from the outside, just like surrounding stones in a game of Go.
annotation.explanation: Mao uses the board game weichi (Go) to illustrate how an invader that strategically encircles China on a map is simultaneously counter-encircled on the ground by rural guerrilla base areas surrounding every occupied city and railway.
annotation.context: Japanese forces held major cities like Taiyuan and railway lines, but could not step into the surrounding countryside controlled by Eighth Route Army base areas.

annotation.targetText: History shows that wars are divided into two kinds, just and unjust. All wars that are progressive are just, and all wars that impede progress are unjust. We Communists oppose all unjust wars that impede progress, but we do not oppose progressive, just wars.
annotation.summary: Marxists distinguish between two types of war: unjust wars of imperialist aggression and oppression, which Communists oppose, and just wars of liberation and progress, which Communists support.
annotation.explanation: Unlike bourgeois pacifism, which condemns all violence in the abstract without examining its class character, Marxism evaluates every war concretely: opposing predatory imperialist wars while actively supporting anti-colonial and revolutionary wars of liberation.
annotation.context: Defending a colonized nation against fascist invasion is fundamentally different from imperialist powers fighting each other to redivide colonies.

annotation.targetText: Ideas, etc. are subjective, while deeds or actions are the subjective translated into the objective, but both represent the dynamic role peculiar to human beings. We term this kind of dynamic role "man's conscious dynamic role", and it is a characteristic that distinguishes man from all other beings.
annotation.summary: While material conditions set the stage and limits of what is possible, conscious human action and strategy are required to turn the possibility of victory into reality.
annotation.explanation: Mao distinguishes dialectical materialism from mechanical fatalism: objective conditions do not automatically produce victory without human agency, planning, and active struggle grounded in objective facts.
annotation.context: Even when an economic crisis weakens the ruling class, social change does not happen automatically unless workers consciously organize and act.

annotation.targetText: It can therefore be said that politics is war without bloodshed while war is politics with bloodshed.
annotation.summary: Politics is conflict without bloodshed, and war is political conflict carried out through bloodshed.
annotation.explanation: Mao condenses the Marxist theory of war: armed conflict is not a purely technical military exercise divorced from class and national politics, but the continuation of political struggle when obstacles cannot be removed by peaceful means.
annotation.context: An army that treats war as purely a matter of weapons and ignores the political needs of the population inevitably loses popular support.

annotation.targetText: The mobilization of the common people throughout the country will create a vast sea in which to drown the enemy, create the conditions that will make up for our inferiority m arms and other things, and create the prerequisites for overcoming every difficulty in the war.
annotation.summary: Politically mobilizing the broad masses creates a vast human sea that overwhelms the invader and overcomes inferior weaponry.
annotation.explanation: Mao argues that military inferiority in weapons is secondary compared to political mobilization; explaining the political aim of the war and linking it to the daily lives of soldiers and peasants turns the entire population into an active force.
annotation.context: Where the Kuomintang relied on passive conscription and censorship, the Communist-led base areas mobilized peasant, women's, and youth associations into active defense.

annotations.chapterTitle: Political Mobilization for the War of Resistance

annotation.targetText: The object of war, namely, the preservation of oneself and the destruction of the enemy, is the essence of war and the basis of all war activities, an essence which pervades all war activities, from the technical to the strategic.
annotation.summary: Every military tactic and strategy boils down to two interrelated goals: preserving one's own forces and destroying the enemy's capacity to resist.
annotation.explanation: Mao traces the dialectical unity of attack and defence from the ancient spear and shield to modern warfare: attack (destroying the enemy) is the primary means of self-preservation, while defence and partial sacrifice serve the preservation of the whole.
annotation.context: Whether a soldier takes cover while firing or a field army retreats to set up an ambush, both actions combine self-preservation with disarming the enemy.

annotation.targetText: In the first and second stages of the war, i.e., in the stages of the enemy's offensive and preservation of his gains, we should conduct tactical offensives within the strategic defensive, campaigns and battles of quick decision within the strategically protracted war, and campaigns and battles on exterior lines within strategically interior lines.
annotation.summary: Within a long defensive war, a weaker army wins by concentrating superior numbers to launch fast, offensive encirclements in individual battles.
annotation.explanation: Mao demonstrates the dialectical inversion between strategy and tactics: strategically China defends over a long war, but tactically on each battlefield China concentrates several divisions against one moving Japanese column to win swift offensive victories.
annotation.context: At the Battle of Pinghsingkuan, the Eighth Route Army ambushed and wiped out an advancing Japanese supply column swiftly before reinforcements could arrive.

annotations.chapterTitle: Offence Within Defence, Quick Decisions Within a Protracted War, Exterior Lines Within Interior Lines

annotation.targetText: The initiative here means an army's freedom of action as distinguished from an enforced loss of freedom. Freedom of action is the very life of an army and, once it is lost, the army is close to defeat or destruction.
annotation.summary: In warfare, the initiative means maintaining freedom of action; a weaker force wrests the initiative from a stronger invader through local superiority, deception, surprise attacks, and mass support.
annotation.explanation: Mao demonstrates that material superiority does not automatically confer the initiative: by organizing the local population to blind the enemy's intelligence and striking unprepared columns, an inferior army forces a superior invader into passivity.
annotation.context: In the anti-Japanese base areas, armed villagers blocked information leaks so effectively that Japanese columns repeatedly marched into Eighth Route Army ambushes.

annotation.targetText: In the great river of absolute fluidity throughout the war there is relative stability at each particular stretch: such is our fundamental view regarding war plans or policies.
annotation.summary: Although battlefield conditions constantly shift, military and political strategy requires plans that remain relatively stable throughout each specific stage of development.
annotation.explanation: Mao applies the dialectical unity of absolute motion and relative rest to strategic planning, refuting both rigid dogmatists who never adapt plans and relativists who reject planning altogether.
annotation.context: While tactical battle plans changed several times a day, the Eighth Route Army's overarching strategic policy of guerrilla and mobile warfare remained stable throughout an entire phase of the war.

annotation.targetText: Guerrilla warfare will not remain the same throughout this long and cruel war, but will rise to a higher level and develop into mobile warfare. Thus the strategic role of guerrilla warfare is twofold, to support regular warfare and to transform itself into regular warfare.
annotation.summary: Guerrilla warfare in a national liberation struggle plays a dual strategic role: supporting the regular army behind enemy lines and gradually growing into regular mobile forces capable of decisive offensives.
annotation.explanation: Mao elevates guerrilla warfare from a purely tactical harassment method to the strategic centerpiece of the second stage of protracted war, showing how dispersed peasant partisan units temper and expand into regular field armies.
annotation.context: By the final stage of the war in 1945, the Communist-led guerrilla units had grown into a regular field force of over one million troops supported by two million militia.

annotations.chapterTitle: Mobile Warfare, Guerrilla Warfare and Positional Warfare

annotation.targetText: Hence campaigns of annihilation are the means of attaining the objective of strategic attrition. In this sense war of annihilation is war of attrition. It is chiefly by using the method of attrition through annihilation that China can wage protracted war.
annotation.summary: A weaker nation wears down a powerful invader strategically (war of attrition) by concentrating forces to wipe out isolated enemy units in individual battles (battles of annihilation).
annotation.explanation: Mao resolves the apparent contradiction between attrition and annihilation: fighting purely defensive battles of attrition drains China's own scarce resources, whereas swiftly encircling and annihilating small enemy columns depletes the enemy while replenishing Chinese arms and morale.
annotation.context: Capturing rifles, artillery, and supplies in short encirclement battles allowed the Eighth Route Army to arm itself directly from Japanese transport columns.

annotations.chapterTitle: War of Attrition and War of Annihilation

annotation.targetText: The landlord class, the bourgeoisie and the warlords of Japan have very serious internal contradictions, which are growing, and the lack of military co-ordination is one of the concrete manifestations of this fact.
annotation.summary: Imperialist powers are never monolithic; internal rivalries among their ruling landlord, capitalist, and military factions inevitably produce strategic blunders that revolutionary forces can exploit.
annotation.explanation: Mao identifies five major operational errors committed by the Japanese command (piecemeal reinforcement, no main direction of attack, lack of coordination, missed opportunities, and failure to annihilate), tracing them to Japan's class contradictions and troop shortages.
annotation.context: Fierce rivalries between Japanese army factions in northern and central China repeatedly prevented coordinated offensives and left vast rural areas unguarded.

annotations.chapterTitle: The Possibilities of Exploiting the Enemy's Mistakes

annotation.targetText: The question of decisive engagements in the anti-Japanese war should be approached from three aspects: we should resolutely fight a decisive engagement in every campaign or battle in which we are sure of victory; we should avoid a decisive engagement in every campaign or battle in which we are not sure of victory; and we should absolutely avoid a strategically decisive engagement on which the fate of the whole nation is staked.
annotation.summary: Revolutionary forces should fight decisive battles only when local victory is assured, avoid battles when conditions are unfavorable, and never gamble the fate of the entire nation on a single all-or-nothing showdown.
annotation.explanation: Mao explains the principle of trading space for time: temporarily giving up a city or territory to preserve the main armed forces prevents the invader from winning a quick decision and ensures the survival of the resistance.
annotation.context: When Kuomintang commanders rashly staked elite divisions in static positional battles early in the war, they suffered catastrophic losses, whereas mobile withdrawals preserved forces for protracted resistance.

annotations.chapterTitle: The Question of Decisive Engagements in the Anti-Japanese War

annotation.targetText: The richest source of power to wage war lies in the masses of the people. It is mainly because of the unorganized state of the Chinese masses that Japan dares to bully us.
annotation.summary: The greatest power in war comes from the organized masses of the people; once the people and the army are united as one, no imperialist invader can defeat them.
annotation.explanation: Mao identifies the organized, politically conscious masses as the ultimate strategic force in people's war: once the peasantry and working people are mobilized and united with their own army, any imperialist invader becomes surrounded like a mad bull in a ring of flames.
annotation.context: In the anti-Japanese base areas, millions of organized peasants provided intelligence, food, recruits, and guerrilla coordination that paralyzed Japanese occupation forces.

annotations.chapterTitle: The Army and the People Are the Foundation of Victory

annotation.targetText: In the eyes of the subjugationists the enemy are supermen and we Chinese are worthless, while in the eyes of the theorists of quick victory we Chinese are supermen and the enemy are worthless. Both are wrong. We take a different view; the War of Resistance Against Japan is a protracted war, and the final victory will be China's.
annotation.summary: Defeatists treat the enemy as invincible supermen while quick-victory dreamers treat the enemy as helpless; realistic materialist analysis shows the war will be long, hard, and ultimately victorious.
annotation.explanation: Mao concludes his lectures by contrasting metaphysical extremes with materialist dialectics, which assesses both the enemy's temporary strength and its fatal long-term contradictions.
annotation.context: Delivered in May and June 1938, Mao's strategic blueprint guided the Chinese resistance through seven more years of war to victory in August 1945.

annotation.targetText: We are confronted with two types of social contradictions : those between ourselves and the enemy and those among the people. The two are totally different in nature.
annotation.summary: Socialist society faces two fundamentally different kinds of conflicts: antagonistic conflicts between the people and their enemies, and non-antagonistic conflicts among the people themselves.
annotation.explanation: Mao introduces his central theoretical innovation for socialist governance: separating hostile class antagonisms against counter-revolutionaries from internal disagreements and structural tensions among the working masses and their allies.
annotation.context: A socialist state must treat foreign-backed sabotage or armed counter-revolution differently from a workplace dispute or policy disagreement among ordinary workers.
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotations.bookTitle: On the Correct Handling of Contradictions Among the People
annotations.chapterTitle: On the Correct Handling of Contradictions Among the People

annotation.targetText: As a matter of fact, freedom and democracy exist not in the abstract, but only in the concrete. In a society where class struggle exists, if there is freedom for the exploiting classes to exploit the working people, there is no freedom for the working people not to be exploited.
annotation.summary: Freedom and democracy are never abstract; in any class society, giving capitalists the freedom to exploit workers automatically denies workers the freedom from exploitation.
annotation.explanation: Mao refutes Western liberal claims of universal, classless democracy, showing that democracy belongs to the political superstructure and always serves a specific economic base and class interest.
annotation.context: In capitalist two-party systems, billionaires can freely fund campaigns and own media monopolies, while workers lack economic security and genuine political representation.
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotations.bookTitle: On the Correct Handling of Contradictions Among the People
annotations.chapterTitle: On the Correct Handling of Contradictions Among the People

annotation.targetText: The only way to settle questions of an ideological nature or controversial issues among the people is by the democratic method, the method of discussion, criticism, persuasion and education, and not by the method of coercion or repression.
annotation.summary: Ideological questions and debates among the people cannot be solved by force or administrative bans; they can only be resolved through open discussion, criticism, persuasion, and education.
annotation.explanation: Because ideological beliefs and questions of right and wrong among the people cannot be forced by decree, Mao insists on patient reasoning, debate, and the 'unity : criticism : unity' method.
annotation.context: Banning a mistaken viewpoint among workers without explaining why it is wrong only drives the idea underground, whereas open discussion builds genuine understanding.

annotations.bookTitle: On the Correct Handling of Contradictions Among the People
annotations.chapterTitle: On the Correct Handling of Contradictions Among the People

annotation.targetText: The class struggle between the proletariat and the bourgeoisie, the class struggle between the various political forces, and the class struggle between the proletariat and the bourgeoisie in the ideological field will still be protracted and tortuous and at times even very sharp.
annotation.summary: Even after socialist ownership is established, the ideological and political struggle between the working class and the bourgeoisie remains long, complex, and at times intense.
annotation.explanation: Even after private ownership of industry and land is largely socialized, bourgeois and petty-bourgeois worldviews persist for decades, requiring ongoing ideological struggle so capitalism is not restored.
annotation.context: In socialist countries, old habits of individualism, careerism, and market mentality continue to influence culture and policy long after factories are nationalized.

annotations.bookTitle: On the Correct Handling of Contradictions Among the People
annotations.chapterTitle: On the Correct Handling of Contradictions Among the People

annotation.targetText: Revisionism, or Right opportunism, is a bourgeois trend of thought that is even more dangerous than dogmatism.
annotation.summary: Revisionism is a bourgeois ideological trend inside the socialist movement that is even more dangerous than dogmatism because it hollows out the core of Marxism from within.
annotation.explanation: Mao warns that while dogmatists apply Marxist phrases mechanically, revisionists pay lip-service to Marxism while attacking its core principles: materialist dialectics, party leadership, and the people's democratic dictatorship.
annotation.context: Political factions that use socialist rhetoric while dismantling public ownership and weakening working-class state power pave the way for capitalist restoration.
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotations.bookTitle: On the Correct Handling of Contradictions Among the People
annotations.chapterTitle: On the Correct Handling of Contradictions Among the People

annotation.targetText: All democratic demands are "unachievable" under imperialism in the sense that politically they are hard to achieve or totally unachievable without a series of revolutions.
annotation.summary: Lenin dismantles the imperialist economism fallacy that claims finance capital makes democratic demands impossible, clarifying that while achieving democracy requires revolutionary mass struggle, political demands remain indispensable for socialist mobilization.
annotation.explanation: Lenin dismantles the imperialist economism fallacy that claims finance capital makes democratic demands impossible, clarifying that while achieving democracy requires revolutionary mass struggle, political demands remain indispensable for socialist mobilization.

annotations.bookTitle: A Caricature of Marxism and Imperialist Economism

annotation.targetText: The social revolution can come only in the form of an epoch in which are combined civil war by the proletariat against the bourgeoisie in the advanced countries and a whole series of democratic and revolutionary movements, including the national liberation movement, in the undeveloped, backward and oppressed nations.
annotation.summary: Lenin outlines the global architecture of socialist revolution: an entire historical epoch that unites working-class revolutions in advanced capitalist states with anti-colonial national liberation revolts in the oppressed periphery.
annotation.explanation: Lenin outlines the global architecture of socialist revolution: an entire historical epoch that unites working-class revolutions in advanced capitalist states with anti-colonial national liberation revolts in the oppressed periphery.
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotations.bookTitle: A Caricature of Marxism and Imperialist Economism

annotation.targetText: Who are our enemies? Who are our friends? This is a question of the first importance for the revolution.
annotation.summary: Revolutionary strategy begins with concrete class analysis to distinguish true allies from class enemies.
annotation.explanation: Mao opens Volume I of his Selected Works by establishing that revolutionary strategy begins with concrete class analysis. Without accurately identifying which social classes have a material interest in overthrowing imperialism and feudalism and which classes benefit from maintaining exploitation, a revolutionary party inevitably isolates itself or surrenders leadership to vacillating bourgeois allies.
annotation.context: In anti-colonial struggles across the Global South, movements that failed to distinguish between national-popular allies and foreign-backed comprador elites were repeatedly betrayed from within once formal independence was achieved.

annotations.bookTitle: Analysis of the Classes in Chinese Society
annotations.chapterTitle: Analysis of the Classes in Chinese Society

annotation.targetText:
The socialist dictatorship of the proletariat, capture of power by the 
proletariat: this is what the socialist revolution must start with.
annotation.summary: The conquest of state power and dictatorship of the proletariat is the necessary starting point of revolution.
annotation.explanation: Socialist revolution cannot bypass state power as anarchists advocate. The working class must capture state power and establish its own dictatorship to suppress counter-revolutionary resistance and expropriate the means of production from the capitalist class.
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotation.targetText: disarming of the workers was the first commandment for the bourgeois at the helm of the state
annotation.summary: Bourgeois state rule demands worker disarming: disarming the armed proletariat is always the primary mandate of the ruling class after every revolution.
annotation.explanation: Engels demonstrates that whenever the working class wins democratic victories through armed struggle, the capitalists prioritize disarming the workers to preserve wage slavery and capitalist property relations.
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotation.targetText: The working men have no country. We cannot take from them what they have not got.
annotation.summary: Because workers hold no property in the nation, their interests cross borders and nationalism cannot unite them with their own employers.
annotation.explanation: The line answers the charge that communists want to abolish countries. Marx and Engels argue that the working class is already stripped of national character by capitalism and that its political supremacy must first be won inside each nation before it can become international.
annotation.context: The slogan underlies the internationalist position that Lenin later used against social chauvinism during the First World War.

annotation.targetText: The proletarians have nothing to lose but their chains. They have a world to win.
annotation.summary: The closing call states that workers have no property interest in the present order and everything to gain from overturning it.
annotation.explanation: The ending contrasts the ruling classes trembling at a communist revolution with a working class that risks only its chains. It fuses the open declaration of aims with the demand for the forcible overthrow of existing social conditions.
annotation.context: Combined with the final slogan 'Working Men of All Countries, Unite!', it became the most reproduced line of the socialist movement.

annotations.chapterTitle: IV. Position of the Communists in Relation to the Various Existing Opposition Parties

annotation.targetText: Leninism is Marxism of the era of imperialism and the proletarian revolution. To be more exact, Leninism is the theory and tactics of the proletarian revolution in general, the theory and tactics of the dictatorship of the proletariat in particular.
annotation.summary: Stalin defines Leninism as Marxism of the era of imperialism and the proletarian revolution.
annotation.explanation: Leninism is not merely a localized Russian doctrine, but the universal development of Marxist theory under 20th-century monopoly capitalism. It synthesizes the theory and tactics of the proletarian revolution and the practical consolidation of the dictatorship of the proletariat.
annotation.context: Delivered at Sverdlov University in Moscow in April 1924 shortly after Lenin's death, as the Bolshevik leadership sought to systematize Marxist-Leninist theory for the thousands of industrial workers joining in the mass "Lenin Enrollment."
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotation.targetText: Some say that Leninism is the application of Marxism to the conditions that are peculiar to the situation in Russia. This definition contains a particle of truth, but not the whole truth by any means. Lenin, indeed, applied Marxism to Russian conditions, and applied it in a masterly way. But if Leninism were only the application of Marxism to the conditions that are peculiar to Russia it would be a purely national and only a national, a purely Russian and only a Russian, phenomenon. We know, however, that Leninism is not merely a Russian, but an international phenomenon rooted in the whole of international development.
annotation.summary: Leninism is an international theoretical system rooted in global imperialist development.
annotation.explanation: Refutes the opportunist claim that Leninism was uniquely tailored for backward Russian conditions. While Lenin applied Marxism masterfully to Russian reality, the core problems he resolved (imperialist war, monopoly trusts, the vanguard party, national liberation) belong to the entire world capitalist system.

annotation.targetText:
Because Russia was the focus of all these contradictions of imperialism.
 
Because Russia, more than any other country, was pregnant with revolution, and she alone, therefore, was in a position to solve those contradictions in a revolutionary way.
annotation.summary: Tsarist Russia concentrated all contradictions of imperialism, making it the flashpoint of world revolution.
annotation.explanation: Russia stood at the junction of brutal capitalist exploitation, colonial oppression in the borderlands, and militarist despotism, while harboring the most militant, revolutionary proletariat. Solving these combined contradictions required breaking the entire chain of international capital.
annotation.context: In 1917, Tsarist Russia was embroiled in catastrophic military defeat, economic collapse, and massive peasant uprisings against landlords, creating a unique historical convergence that propelled the Bolsheviks to power.

annotations.chapterTitle: I. The Historical Roots of Leninism

annotation.targetText: Firstly, the testing of the theoretical dogmas of the Second International in the crucible of the revolutionary struggle of the masses, in the crucible of living practice: that is to say, the restoration of the broken unity between theory and practice, the healing of the rift between them; for only in this way can a truly proletarian party armed with revolutionary theory be created.
annotation.summary: Leninism restores the unity of theory and practice against Second International dogmatism.
annotation.explanation: The Second International reduced Marxism to dry, academic formulas and parliamentary routine divorced from actual revolutionary struggle. Lenin re-established the vital link between theoretical science and mass action, insisting that all dogma must be tested and forged in the living furnace of practical mass revolution.
annotation.context: In August 1914, the dominant leaders of the Second International abandoned anti-militarist resolutions to vote for national war credits in World War I, prompting Lenin to break irrevocably with their reformist opportunism.

annotation.targetText: This is why Lenin said that "revolutionary theory is not a dogma," that it "assumes final shape only in close connection with the practical activity of a truly mass and truly revolutionary movement" ("Left-Wing" Communism3); for theory must serve practice, for "theory must answer the questions raised by practice" (What the "Friends of the People" Are 4), for it must be tested by practical results.
annotation.summary: Marxist theory is not a rigid dogma, but a living guide to mass revolutionary action.
annotation.explanation: Theory assumes definitive scientific shape only in unbreakable connection with the concrete struggles of the working masses. Theory must answer the questions raised by practice, and practice must be enlightened by revolutionary theory.

annotation.targetText:
"Without a revolutionary theory there can be no revolutionary movement"1 (see Vol. IV, p. 380). 

Lenin, better than anyone else, understood the great importance of theory, particularly for a party such as ours, in view of the vanguard fighter of the international proletariat which has fallen to its lot, and in view of the complicated internal and international situation in which it finds itself.
annotation.summary: Without revolutionary theory there can be no revolutionary movement.
annotation.explanation: Quotes Lenin to emphasize that spontaneous working-class anger alone cannot overthrow capitalism. Only a disciplined vanguard party armed with scientific socialist theory can perceive the laws of historical development and lead the proletariat to political power.

annotation.targetText: The front of capital will be pierced where the chain of imperialism is weakest, for the proletarian revolution is the result of the breaking of the chain of the world imperialist front at its weakest link; and it may turn out that the country which has started the revolution, which has made a breach in the front of capital, is less developed in a capitalist sense than other, more developed, countries, which have, however, remained within the framework of capitalism.
annotation.summary: The imperialist front breaks at its weakest link, not necessarily where industry is most advanced.
annotation.explanation: Rejects the mechanical determinism of Second International theorists who claimed socialist revolution could only occur in the most advanced Western economies. In the era of interconnected global imperialism, the revolutionary rupture occurs where imperialist contradictions and political fragility are most acutely concentrated.

annotation.targetText: dictatorship of the proletariat is not a mere change of personalities in the government, a change of the cabinet," etc., leaving the old economic and political order intact.
annotation.summary: The dictatorship of the proletariat requires smashing the bourgeois state, not a mere change of cabinet.
annotation.explanation: Socialist revolution cannot simply inherit existing capitalist parliaments, courts, and police bureaucracies. The working class must smash the old state machine and erect a new proletarian state capable of expropriating the capitalists and defending workers power.
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotations.chapterTitle: IV. The Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotation.targetText:
Soviet power as the state form of the dictatorship of the proletariat. 

1) The dictatorship of the proletariat as the instrument of the proletarian revolution.
annotation.summary: Soviet power is the state form of the dictatorship of the proletariat.
annotation.explanation: The Soviet form of governance unites working-class political representation with immediate economic administration, providing the historic political structure through which the working masses organize society, suppress counter-revolution, and build socialism.
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotations.chapterTitle: IV. The Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotation.targetText: The fundamental question of Leninism, its point of departure, is not the peasant question, but the question of the dictatorship of the proletariat, of the conditions under which it can be achieved, of the conditions under which it can be consolidated. The peasant question, as the question of the ally of the proletariat in its struggle for power, is a derivative question.
annotation.summary: The peasant question is the question of the strategic ally of the proletariat in the struggle for power.
annotation.explanation: The fundamental objective of Leninism is the proletarian dictatorship. The peasant question is vital as a derivative of that goal: without the revolutionary alliance between industrial workers and working peasants, the proletariat cannot successfully seize or retain state power.
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotation.targetText: Formerly, the national question was usually confined to a narrow circle of questions, concerning, primarily, "civilised" nationalities. The Irish, the Hungarians, the Poles, the Finns, the Serbs, and several other European nationalities: that was the circle of unequal peoples in whose destinies the leaders of the Second International were interested. The scores and hundreds of millions of Asiatic and African peoples who are suffering national oppression in its most savage and cruel form usually remained outside of their field of vision. They hesitated to put white and black, "civilised" and "uncivilised" on the same plane. Two or three meaningless, lukewarm resolutions, which carefully evaded the question of liberating the colonies: that was all the leaders of the Second International could boast of. Now we can say that this duplicity and half-heartedness in dealing with the national question has been brought to an end. Leninism laid bare this crying incongruity, broke down the wall between whites and blacks, between European and Asiatics, between the "civilised" and "uncivilised" slaves of imperialism, and thus linked the national question with the question of the colonies. The national question was thereby transformed from a particular and internal state problem into a general and international problem, into a world problem of emancipating the oppressed peoples in the dependent countries and colonies from the yoke of imperialism.
annotation.summary: Leninism transforms the national question into the global struggle of colonial peoples against imperialism.
annotation.explanation: Second International theorists treated national rights as a domestic European legal problem. Leninism tore down the barrier between European and colonized peoples, uniting the national liberation struggles in Asia, Africa, and Latin America directly with the international proletarian socialist movement.

annotation.targetText: Strategy is the determination of the direction of the main blow of the proletariat at a given stage of the revolution, the elaboration of a corresponding plan for the disposition of the revolutionary forces (main and secondary reserves), the fight to carry out this plan throughout the given stage of the revolution.
annotation.summary: Strategy determines the direction of the main blow of the proletariat across a historic revolutionary stage.
annotation.explanation: Defines strategy as the overarching plan for aligning class forces, selecting principal and secondary reserves, and directing mass energy toward decisive political objectives at each historical phase of the revolutionary struggle.

annotation.targetText: Tactics are the determination of the line of conduct of the proletariat in the comparatively short period of the flow or ebb of the movement, of the rise or decline of the revolution, the fight to carry out this line by means of replacing old forms of struggle and organisation by new ones, old slogans by new ones, by combining these forms, etc. While the object of strategy is to win the war against tsarism, let us say, or against the bourgeoisie, to carry through the struggle against tsarism or against the bourgeoisie to its end, tactics pursue less important objects, for their aim is not the winning of the war as a whole, but the winning of some particular engagements or some particular battles, the carrying through successfully of some particular campaigns or actions corresponding to the concrete circumstances in the given period of rise or decline of the revolution.
annotation.summary: Tactics govern the concrete line of conduct during short-term ebbs and flows of the mass movement.
annotation.explanation: Tactics adapt organizational forms, agitation slogans, and immediate methods of struggle to fluctuating political conditions, seeking to win specific battles and prepare forces for decisive strategic confrontations.

annotation.targetText: The Party must be, first of all, the advanced detachment of the working class. The Party must absorb all the best elements of the working class, their experience, their revolutionary spirit, their selfless devotion to the cause of the proletariat.
annotation.summary: The Party as the advanced detachment of the working class: vanguard armed with revolutionary consciousness.
annotation.explanation: The party gathers the most dedicated, class-conscious, and theoretically trained members of the working class. It acts as an ideological beacon and organized general staff, leading the broader masses toward socialist revolution without detaching itself from them.

annotation.targetText: The Party as the embodiment of unity of will, unity incompatible with the existence of factions. The achievement and maintenance of the dictatorship of the proletariat is impossible without a party which is strong by reason of its solidarity and iron discipline.
annotation.summary: Party unity of will is incompatible with the existence of factionalism.
annotation.explanation: Maintains that achieving and sustaining the dictatorship of the proletariat requires iron organizational discipline and singular unity of will. Factions create rival centers of power that dissolve discipline, paralyze decision-making, and weaken the workers state.
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotation.targetText:
The combination of Russian revolutionary sweep with American efficiency is the essence of Leninism in Party and state work.

This combination alone produces the finished type of Leninist worker, the style of Leninism in work.
annotation.summary: Leninist style in work combines Russian revolutionary sweep with American efficiency.
annotation.explanation: Revolutionary enthusiasm without practical discipline degenerates into idle fantasy and bureaucratic scheme-making; practical efficiency without revolutionary vision degenerates into narrow, unprincipled technocracy. The complete communist organizer unifies bold revolutionary ideals with rigorous, practical execution.

annotation.targetText: our hostilities must have a clearly defined political goal and firmly established political responsibilities.
annotation.summary: Guerrilla war must serve a clear political goal and rest on firm political responsibility.
annotation.explanation: Mao says that because the resistance is that of a semi-colonial country against imperialism, military action cannot be separated from politics. The creation of a national united front gives the guerrillas their direction.
annotation.context: It sums up the principle that people's war is a political war carried out with military means.

annotation.targetText: A primary feature of guerrilla operations is their dependence upon the people themselves to organize battalions and other units.
annotation.summary: Guerrilla forces are organised by and from the local population.
annotation.explanation: Unlike regular units, guerrilla organisation depends on local circumstances and on the people's own initiative, which is what makes them hard for an invader to destroy.
annotation.context: This is the basis of the later slogan that the guerrilla moves among the people as fish in water.

annotations.chapterTitle: The Relation Of Guerrilla Hostilitiesto Regular Operations

annotation.targetText: These people will not admit the fundamental necessity for guerrilla bands that spring from the armed people.
annotation.summary: Critics of corrupt guerrilla bands fail to see that real guerrilla forces must arise from the armed population.
annotation.explanation: Mao answers those who judge guerrilla warfare by undisciplined units that were used as cover for bribery and corruption, saying proper guerrilla bands spring from the people and must be given proper political leadership.
annotation.context: Discipline and political education are treated as conditions for a guerrilla force to keep the people's support.

annotations.chapterTitle: The Relation Of Guerrilla Hostilitiesto Regular Operations

annotation.targetText:
This article will express our views on guerrilla warfare and its correct
utilization. Above all, we must emphasize at the outset that this form of
struggle is a means to an end. That end, essential and inevitable for any
revolutionary, is the conquest of political power.
annotation.summary: Guerrilla warfare is not an end in itself, but an instrument for the revolutionary conquest of political power.
annotation.explanation: Guerrilla fighting is neither a romantic adventure nor a self-sufficient military objective. It is a specific political method of armed struggle employed by an oppressed people to destroy the repressive state apparatus of the ruling class and establish revolutionary workers and peasants power.
annotation.context: Written in September 1963 for Cuba Socialista following the 1959 victory of the Cuban Revolution, addressing debates among Latin American communist parties over armed struggle versus peaceful electoral paths.
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotation.targetText:
The subjective conditions in each country, the factors of revolutionary
consciousness, organization and leadership, can accelerate or delay
revolution, depending on the state of their development. Sooner or
later in each historic epoch objective conditions ripen, consciousness
is acquired, organization is achieved, leadership arises, and revolution
takes place.
annotation.summary: Subjective conditions of leadership and organization determine whether maturing objective crises erupt into successful revolution.
annotation.explanation: While extreme exploitation and economic crises provide the objective basis for revolution, they do not automatically produce revolutionary change. A dedicated political-military vanguard must actively develop subjective consciousness and organize the masses to seize historical opportunities.
annotation.context: Reflects the core premise of foco theory: that a committed revolutionary nucleus can help create the subjective conditions for revolution rather than waiting passively for crisis conditions to spontaneously organize themselves.
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotation.targetText:
As Fidel has said, the cordillera of the Andes will be the Sierra Maestra
of Latin America; and the immense territories this continent encompasses
will become the scene of a life or death struggle against imperialism.
annotation.summary: Anti-imperialist liberation in the Americas is continental in scope, demanding international solidarity across borders.
annotation.explanation: Because United States imperialism operates across national boundaries to coordinate military interventions and prop up military dictatorships throughout the hemisphere, individual national revolutions cannot remain isolated. The liberation of Latin America demands coordinated continental solidarity and anti-imperialist struggle.
annotation.context: Echoes the Second Declaration of Havana (1962), forecasting the continental spread of national liberation movements across the Andes and Central America.

annotation.targetText: It is the most ardent wish of the author that this book should soon be transformed from a weapon against imperialism into an historic document relegated to the archives.
annotation.summary: Written as a theoretical weapon against world imperialism, Bukharin looks forward to the complete overthrow of capitalism.
annotation.explanation: Writing immediately after the Bolshevik seizure of power in November 1917, Bukharin connects theoretical economic analysis directly to the practical revolutionary struggle to abolish imperialism.

annotation.targetText: For, until the world socialist revolution breaks out, until it embraces several countries and is strong enough to overcome international imperialism, it is the direct duty of the socialists who have conquered in one country (especially a backward one) not to accept battle against the giants of imperialism. Their duty is to try to avoid battle, to wait until the conflicts between the imperialists weaken them even more, and bring the revolution in other countries even nearer.
annotation.summary: A newly victorious socialist state encircled by stronger imperialist powers must avoid premature military battle and utilize inter-imperialist contradictions.
annotation.explanation: Defending the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk against the Left Communists, Lenin shows that preserving the revolutionary state requires sober material calculation rather than walking into a military trap set by stronger imperialist powers.

annotations.chapterTitle: I. The Brest Peace and the Balance of Forces

annotation.targetText: It is in the interest of capital to destroy its enemy (the revolutionary proletariat) bit by bit, before the workers in all countries have united (actually united, i.e., by beginning the revolution). It is in our interest to do all that is possible, to take advantage of the slightest opportunity to postpone the decisive battle until the moment (or until after the moment) the revolutionary workers’ contingents have united in a single great international army.
annotation.summary: Strategic retreat and playing for time protect an isolated socialist revolution from being crushed piecemeal by international capital.
annotation.explanation: Lenin shows that genuine proletarian internationalism requires preserving the existing bastion of socialist power until revolutionary movements in other countries mature.

annotations.chapterTitle: II. Proletarian Defencism and Revolutionary Phrase-Making

annotation.targetText: On the one hand, it would be a fatal mistake to declare that since there is a discrepancy between our economic “forces” and our political strength, it “follows” that we should not have seized power.[4] Such an argument can be advanced only by a “man in a muffler”,[5] who forgets that there will always be such a “discrepancy”, that it always exists in the development of nature as well as in the development of society, that only by a series of attempts: each of which, taken by itself, will be one sided and will suffer from certain inconsistencies: will complete socialism be created by the revolutionary co-operation of the proletarians of all countries.
annotation.summary: Refusing to seize political power until economic conditions are 'perfect' is mechanical dogmatism; uneven development is universal in nature and history.
annotation.explanation: Lenin refutes both Menshevik determinism (which claimed Russia was too economically backward for revolution) and ultra-left impatience, showing that proletarian state power can be used to consciously accelerate material development.
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotations.chapterTitle: V. Compromises, Labour Discipline, and Socialist Construction

annotation.targetText: Whoever brings about even the slightest weakening of the iron discipline of the party of the proletariat (especially during its dictatorship), is actually aiding the bourgeoisie against the proletariat.
annotation.summary: Bolshevik party discipline was not maintained through blind obedience, but through vanguard class-consciousness, deep ties to working people, and practical tactical success.
annotation.explanation: Bolshevik party discipline was not maintained through blind obedience, but through vanguard class-consciousness, deep ties to working people, and practical tactical success.

annotations.chapterTitle: “Left-Wing” Communism in Germany: The Leaders, the Party, the Class, the Masses

annotation.targetText: No Compromises? In the quotation from the Frankfurt pamphlet, we have seen how emphatically the “Lefts” have advanced this slogan.
annotation.summary: Dogmatically rejecting all tactical compromises ties the hands of the revolutionary party in complex class struggles.
annotation.explanation: Distinguishing between necessary tactical compromises that preserve organizational strength vs. opportunist surrenders of principle is essential for political leadership.

annotation.targetText:
“The German Communists are Communists because, through all the intermediate stations and all compromises created, not by them but by the course of historical development, they clearly perceive and constantly pursue the final aim; the abolition of classes and the creation of a society in which there will no longer be private ownership of land or of the means of production. The thirty-three Blanquists are Communists just because they imagine that, merely because they want to skip the intermediate stations and compromises, the matter is settled, and if ‘it begins’ in the next few days; which they take for granted; and they take over power, ‘communism will be introduced’ the day after tomorrow. If that is not immediately possible, they are not Communists.

“What childish innocence it is to present one’s own impatience as a theoretically convincing argument!”
annotation.summary: Engels and Lenin critique Blanquist ultra-leftism for mistaking revolutionary impatience for Marxist strategy.
annotation.explanation: Quoting Engels against the Blanquist Communards, Lenin shows that dogmatically rejecting all intermediate steps and tactical compromises is childish impatience rather than scientific socialism.

annotation.targetText: Science demands, first, that the experience of other countries be taken into account, especially if these other countries, which are also capitalist, are undergoing, or have recently undergone, a very similar experience; second, it demands that account be taken of all the forces, groups, parties, classes and masses operating in a given country, and also that policy should not be determined only by the desires and views, by the degree of class-consciousness and the militancy of one group or party alone.
annotation.summary: Revolutionary strategy must be grounded in an objective analysis of all class forces, not the subjective militancy of an ultra-left minority.
annotation.explanation: Lenin contrasts scientific socialism with ultra-left voluntarism, showing that communists cannot base their tactics merely on their own hatred of bourgeois politicians while ignoring where the majority of workers currently stand.

annotation.targetText: “The Communist Party must not compromise. . . . The Communist Party must keep its doctrine pure, and its independence of reformism inviolate, its mission is to lead the way, without stopping or turning, by the direct road to the communist revolution.”
annotation.summary: Ultra-leftism treats doctrinal purity as a substitute for winning over the working-class majority through practical political experience.
annotation.explanation: Distinguishing between necessary tactical compromises that preserve organizational strength vs. opportunist surrenders of principle is essential for political leadership.

annotation.targetText: To act otherwise would mean hampering the cause of the revolution, since revolution is impossible without a change in the views of the majority of the working class, a change brought about by the political experience of the masses, never by propaganda alone.
annotation.summary: The working masses cannot be won to revolution by propaganda alone; they must learn through their own practical political experience.
annotation.explanation: Lenin explains why ultra-left abstentionism fails: when a small revolutionary minority refuses to engage with mass organizations or elections, it abandons the masses instead of helping them see through reformist leaders in practice.

annotation.targetText: Let them try to prepare for (and then implement) the dictatorship of the proletariat, without a rigorously centralised party with iron discipline, without the ability to become masters of every sphere, every branch, and every variety of political and cultural work.
annotation.summary: Bolshevik party discipline was not maintained through blind obedience, but through vanguard class-consciousness, deep ties to working people, and practical tactical success.
annotation.explanation: Bolshevik party discipline was not maintained through blind obedience, but through vanguard class-consciousness, deep ties to working people, and practical tactical success.
